records.raw_text: “Light and Medium Merchant Mill”  (LMMM)  comprises  of  two  mills,  namely
Billet mill and Bar mill, situated at + 5 m. level. Billet  mill,  which  is
also called as “Break Down Mill” (BDM), converts blooms  of  320mm  x  250mm
cross section and 6.1 – 6.35 mt length, in to billets of size  125mm  x  125
mm square cross section. The  Billet  Mill  supplies  feed  material,  i.e.,
billets to both Bar Mill and Wire Rod Mill  (WRM).  The  Bar  mill  produces
finished long product of various sections ranging from  16mm  to  36mm  size
Rebars & Rounds and other structural products like Angles and Channels.
Billet mill is a hot rolling mill with 7 stands ( 4 horizontal  and  3
vertical). The heating of blooms to nearly 1200° C is done by two  furnaces,
namely “Walking Beam Furnaces”. Usually, one furnace is designated  for  WRM
rolling and another for Bar mill.
“Walking  Beam  Furnace”  (WBF)  is  one  of  its  kind,  that  allows
continuous charging and continuous discharging of blooms while bringing  320
x 250 mm blooms to rolling temperature. The walking beam  mechanism  ensures
smooth movement of skids and posts, in side  the  furnace.  This  gas  fired
furnace uses the mixed  gas  of  gases  produced  and  supplied  from  Blast
furnace, Cokeovens and Steel Melting Shop. It also has a  provision  to  use
oil as fuel, in case of exigencies.
In order to save energy and also to cool  the  furnaces  by  utilising
the latent heat, mill has been provided  with  evaporative  cooling  system,
which consists of a steam separating drum and cooling circuits  with  a  re-
The blooms that are soaked in the Walking beam furnaces are rolled  in
Billet mill to produce billets of  125mm  x  125mm  cross  section.  Billets
meant for Bar Mill are cropped at the front  end  and  rear  end  by  flying
shear and are sent directly to Bar Mill for rolling,  as  both  Billet  Mill
and Bar Mill are in same rolling line.
Billets meant for WRM are cut in to 3 lengths by flying shear and  are
pushed on to one of the two “Turn  Over  Type  Cooling  Beds”  (TOTCBs)  for
cooling. Later, they lifted with the help of EOT cranes at the  end  of  the
TOCB, after cooling, and stacked at Billets Loading and Dispatch (BLD)  area
The Bar Mill also is a hot rolling mill with a series of stands  (both
horizontal and vertical) to convert billets  of  125mm  x  125  mm  size  to
finished product as per  the  schedule  given  by  Production  Planning  and
Bar mill consists of 3 groups, namely,  Roughing  group,  Intermediate
group and Finishing group. Bar Mill is a two-line  mill,  though,  initially
has a single roughing group in common,  with  two  strands,  to  accommodate
rolling of two billets simultaneously for two lines. There are 8  stands  in
roughing group, five stands each in 2 lines  of  intermediate  group  and  4
stands each in 2 lines of Finishing group.
The “Roller Hearth Furnace” of Bar Mill provides  initial  soaking  of
billets to keep the temperature  alive  during  rolling  in  Bar  Mill.  The
billets are fed from Billet Mill with a continuous feed in to the two  lines
of Bar Mill, alternatively. The billets  pass  through  the  stands  of  all
three groups (Roughing, Intermediate & Finishing) to shape them in  to  bars
of desired section. The bars produced are cut to set length by “cooling  bed
shear” and are sent on to cooling bed for cooling. There  are  “cooling  bed
shears” and “cooling beds” on both the lines separately.
Production of TMT bars is achieved with the help of  Tempcore  cooling
process. Tempcore process involves cooling of  rebars  to  fetch  additional
mechanical properties. This process of conditioning rebars is  a  remarkable
The cooling bed provides air cooling of the bars by means of fans. The
bars are shifted to the end of cooling beds  while  they  are  cooled  down,
with moving rake mechanism.  At  the  end  of  cooling  bed,  the  bars  are
collected in batches and are moved to “Finishing Area” by  means  of  roller
In case of  structurals,  i.e.,  angles  and  channels,  straightening
machines are used to straighten them in cold condition. The  Finishing  area
collects bars in batches, cut them to customer length and bundle  them  with
set number of bars in each bundle. Two “Cold shears” provided separately  on
each line cut the product to the required customer length.  It  is  designed
to cut all sections with a length of 5 m to 24 m. The bars  are  then  moved
to bundling section  by  means  of  chains,  where  they  are  bundled  with
specified number of bars in each bundle, with the help of  binding  machines
and strapping activity. Tags with details of the  product  are  attached  to
Weighing of the bundles is done with the help of on line Roller  table
weigh-bridges and are sent to unloading grids for lifting  to  “Bar  Product
Storage Area” (BPSY), with the help of EOT cranes.
Major Facilities & Salient features of LMMM
1.  Billet Mill and Bar Mill are in same line.
2. Walking Beam Furnaces for continuous and effective heating of blooms in
3. Evaporative cooling system for waste heat recovery in Billet Mill.
4. Turn Over Type Cooling Bed for uniform cooling  of  Billets  in  Billet
5. Tempcore cooling system for achieving mechanical properties  of  Rebars
6. Multi level PLC system for mill control in both  Billet  Mill  and  Bar

2. Title of the QC project: Modification of Vertical Stand Lifting Output
Bar Mill of LMMM is a continuous rolling Mill wherein the material  is  made
to pass through a series of horizontal  and  vertical  stands  in  order  to
obtain a desired profile. In vertical stands, the stand  housing  is  placed
on a platform called lift table.
The lift table is moved up or down by means  of  two  lift  table  gearboxes
driven by a motor. The gearboxes  have  a  central  spindle  which  actually
touches and moves the lift table.  At  the  top,  the  threaded  spindle  is
covered by a bellow to prevent the entry of water, dust, scale, sludge  etc.
into the threads. Bellows  are  directly  fixed  to  the  canopy  body  with
hexagonal headed bolts. Bolts are getting damaged due to directly fixing  of
bolts in the canopy, which is a  thin  plate  of  6mm  approx.  The  foreign
material thus enters into the threads and  then  into  the  gearbox.  It  is
observed that delay occurred due to  break  down  of  Lift  gearbox  spindle
To overcome the aforementioned problem, a flange was fabricated  with  holes
and welded to a pipe. This was welded directly to both  the  bellow  seating
area of the canopy. Now bellows are easily fixed to the modified parts.
With this implementation for six vertical stands,  reduced  delay  in  pass
change due to break downs regarding lift movement of vertical stands.
Invention: The idea is innovative and has improved working conditions. It
is an improvisation of present working condition and method.

विश्वकर्मा राष्ट्रीय पुरस्कार (वी आर पी) का उद्देश्य उनके कामगारों या समूहों को मान्यता देना है, जो कारखाना अधिनियम 1948, गोदी कामगार (सुरक्षा, स्वास्थ्य और कल्याण) अधिनियम, 1986 परमाणु ऊर्जा नियामक बोर्ड के अधीन संस्थापन तथा भवन और अन्य निर्माण कामगार (रोजगार का विनियमन और सेवा शर्तें) अधिनियम, 1996 के अंतर्गत आते हैं तथा जहाँ उनके सुझाव से उत्पादकता, व्यावसायिक सुरक्षा एवं स्वास्थ्य, पर्यावरण और कार्य परिस्थितियों तथा उत्पाद की गुणवत्ता एवं सुरक्षा में सुधार होता है|

1.विश्वकर्मा राष्ट्रीय पुरस्कार, 2015 के लिए निष्पादन वर्ष 2015 (जनवरी से दिसंबर) माना जाएगा|  अतः केवल 2015 (1 जनवरी-31 दिसंबर, 2015) में दिए गए कार्यान्वित सुझावों वाले आवेदन पत्रों पर ही विचार किया जाएगा|

2.जो संगठन इस योजना में अपना आवेदन पत्र भेजे, उस संगठन में सुझाव योजना (आवेदन पत्र में लिखा जाए) क्रियान्वित होनी चाहिए तथा प्रबंधकों द्वारा निष्पादन वर्ष 2015 में सुझाव मूल्यांकित, स्वीकृत, क्रियान्वित एवं पुरस्कृत किया गया हो|
3.यह योजना केवल कामगारों और पर्यवेक्षकों के लिए है|  प्रबंधक/कार्यपालक व्यक्तिगत या संयुक्त रूप से आवेदन नहीं कर सकते हैं|
4.कार्यान्वित और पुरस्कृत सुझाव से निम्नलिखित में से कोई एक या अधिक लाभ हुआ हो:-

उत्पादकता में सुधार, प्रक्रियाओं में दक्षता, प्रणालियों और प्रक्रियाओं, सामग्री रखरखाव, कीमतों में कमी, उत्पादन और सेवाओं की गुणवत्ता, पैकिंग प्रणाली, सुरक्षा, स्वास्थ्य और पर्यावरण और कार्य परिस्थितियाँ, या/और संयंत्रों/उपकरणों के प्रयोग में सुधार|
कार्यान्वित सुझावों के परिणाम स्वरूप सभी सामग्री में कमी, माल खराब न करना, श्रम की कीमत में कमी, प्रचालन लागत में कमी, भौतिक और मानसिक तनाव में कमी आई हो|
इन सुझावों के कार्यान्वित होने पर स्वदेशी संयंत्र/मशीनरी/पुर्जों का प्रयोग हुआ हो, जिससे विदेशी मुद्रा की बचत हुई हो|

श्रम एवं रोजगार मंत्रालय, भारत सरकार द्वारा त्रिपक्षीय पुरस्कार समिति का गठन किया जाता है, जिसमें कर्मचारी, नियोक्ता और सरकारी प्रतिनिधि शामिल होते हैं| इस समिति का उद्देश्य श्रेणी ‘क’, श्रेणी ‘ख’ और श्रेणी ‘ग’ के पुरस्कारों का निर्णय करना है|  इन तीन वर्गों के अंतर्गत कुल 28 पुरस्कार हैं|  श्रेणी ’क’ में पुरस्कारों की संख्या 05 हैं, प्रत्येक को ` 75,000/-, श्रेणी ‘ख’ में पुरस्कारों की संख्या 08 हैं, प्रत्येक को ` 50,000/- और श्रेणी ‘ग’ में पुरस्कारों की संख्या 15 हैं, प्रत्येक को ` 25,000/- दिए जाते हैं|  नकद पुरस्कार के अतिरिक्त विजेताओं को प्रशस्ति पत्र भी दिया जाता है|

ऊपर दिए गए विजेताओं की संख्या प्रत्येक श्रेणी में कम भी हो सकती है|  यह पुरस्कार समिति सदस्यों के निर्णय पर निर्भर होगा|  पुरस्कार समिति/सरकार का निर्णय अंतिम होगा|  भारत सरकार को यह अधिकार होगा कि वह किसी भी विजेता के सुझाव को, यदि आवश्यक समझे, तो अन्य संगठनों के हित में प्रकाशित कर सकती है|
हरेक आवेदन पत्र के साथ एक ही सुझाव भेजें|  इस योजना के अंतर्गत प्रत्येक कंपनी केवल दस आवेदन ही प्रस्तुत कर सकती है|

अनुलग्नकों/दस्तावेज और प्रविष्ट शुल्क के रूप में ‘सचिव, विश्वकर्मा राष्ट्रीय पुरस्कार समिति’ के नाम से, मुंबई के किसी अनुसूचित बैंक में देय ` 200/- के डिमांड ड्राफ्ट के साथ विधिवत भरा हुआ आवेदन पत्र निम्न पते पर अंतिम तारीख 15.10.2016 तक या उससे पहले भेज दें:

किसी भी प्रकार के अपूर्ण आवेदन पत्र अस्वीकृत कर दिए जाएँगे| सभी आवेदन पत्रों के साथ “सुझाव सारांश” की एक हार्ड कॉपी तथा एक सी.डी. आवेदन पत्र के भाग- II के अनुसार एवं संबंधित ड्राइंग/फोटो, वित्तीय लाभ, गणनाओं आदि सहित होनी चाहिए|
आवेदन शुल्क वापस नहीं किया जाएगा|  आवेदन शुल्क के लिए कोई रसीद नहीं दी जाएगी|

LEGAL ASPECTS OF TENDERS AND CONTRACTS

The object of Law of Contracts is to ensure that the parties to a contract get what they are promised under the contracts they enter into and if not, they are compensated for the loss caused by non-performance of contracts. The Contract Act 1872 deals with Law of Contracts. The Contract Act defines a Contract as "an agreement enforceable by Law". An agreement is nothing but a promise or a set of promises forming consideration for each other. An offer which is accepted becomes a promise. The Contract Act uses the expression 'proposal' which is synonymous to 'offer'. When one person signifies his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other to such act or abstinence, he is said to make a proposal. If the proposal is accepted, it becomes a promise. Acceptance means giving assent or consent, by the party to whom proposal is made, to the proposal made to him.
An agreement, in order to become a contract, must satisfy the following conditions:
Parties must be competent to contract.
The object of the agreement must be lawful.
The agreement should be of such nature that it is not expressly declared as void.

The Contract Act deals with the provisions relating to formation of contract besides dealing with performance, breach, impossibility of performance, quasi contracts, remedies for breach of contract, indemnity and guarantee, bailments and agency.
LEGAL ASPECTS OF CONTRACTS INVOLVING PUBLIC BODIES

The first step in entering into a contract where a public sector undertaking is one of the parties is to issue a notice inviting tender either for supply of goods or services or for disposal of any items or for execution of any building or engineering contract or for execution of any major project. Only such contracts which do not involve much cost can be finalised without formally inviting tenders. Most of the public bodies have standardised their tender documents. Tender documents normally contain the general terms and conditions of contract common to all the contracts as well as special conditions applicable to the particular work for which NIT has been issued. Invitation to tender issued by public bodies is not an offer but it is an invitation to the contractors to make their offers.

When a contractor submits his tender, he is said to make a proposal or an offer. While most of the public bodies require the offerors to submit their offers in the tender formats prescribed by them, there is nothing in law to prevent the tenderers from deviating the conditions mentioned in tender documents and lay down their own terms and conditions. When such a tender with deviations is received, it is for the public body which has issued NIT to decide whether to accept such offer or not depending on the nature and extent of deviations.
TENDER RECEIVED AFTER THE PRESCRIBED DATE:

Normally public bodies should avoid accepting tender received after the prescribed date. However, in exceptional circumstances like poor response to tender or when the delay is bonafide, late tender can be accepted. However, in such cases, it is necessary for the public body to give a fresh notification extending time for receiving tender so that if any other tenderer wants to submit the tender, he can do so before the extended date.
WHETHER TENDER SHOULD ALWAYS BE TREATED AS AN OFFER:

Suppose a public body invites tender and it receives a good response. Out of the tenders received, suppose a particular tender is fit for acceptance. If acceptance is communicated without any modifications to tender, it ripens into a contract. However, if the tender does not indicate that the tenderer is willing to do particular action (like sale of goods, or purchase of goods or completion of some works) but simply contains a quotation of prices, then the tender is not an offer but it amounts to an invitation to make offer by the other party. In response to such tender, if any communication is given by the public body which has originally invited the tender, such communication amounts to an offer only but not acceptance. It is for the person who has submitted the tender with mere quotation of price whether to accept the offer made by the public body or not. Sometimes, the tenderer submits a clear offer but the public body which has received the tender does not accept it in toto but imposes several conditions or makes several modifications to tender. In such a case, the communication given by the public body amounts to a counter-offer and it is for the original tenderer whether to accept the counter-offer or not.

Sometimes, a peculiar situation emerges. A contractor submits his tender which is worded like a clear offer. The public body accepts the tender without any modifications but at the end of the acceptance letter, it is mentioned that the contractor should submit his acceptance within a certain time. A question arises whether the contract is completed between the parties or whether the contractor has the option of accepting it or not. It is submitted that in such a situation, the public body is not deemed to have accepted the original tender but is deemed to have given it's own offer (may be similar to the offer made by the contractor). Then the contractor has the right either to accept the offer of the public body or to reject it.

Sometimes, a public body may communicate its clear acceptance to the offer of the contractor but mentions in the acceptance letter that the contract is required to be executed in a formal document signed by both the parties. In such a case, the contract is not completed unless a formal document is executed and signed by both the parties. However, there may be some circumstances to show that the public body never wanted the formal document to be a condition precedent for formation of contract notwithstanding the fact that there is a reference to execution of formal document in the acceptance letter. For example, a public body allows the contractor to start the work and also performs some obligations on its part.

If a public body expects the contractors to follow a particular procedure in submitting the tender, the public body also should follow its own procedure laid down in the matter of acceptance of tender. A public body does not have the same discretion as a private body or an individual employer. If some qualifications have been prescribed for tenderers at the time of issuing the invitation to tender, a public body cannot favourably consider a tender of a contractor who has not fulfilled the prescribed qualifications.
CAN A TENDERER REVOKE HIS TENDER:
Under section 5 of the Contract Act, a proposal can be revoked at any time before the communication of acceptance is complete as against the offeror.

The communication of acceptance as against the offeror is complete the moment the acceptance is put in a course of transmission to him, so as to be out of the power of the acceptor. So, before the acceptance is put in a course of transmission, an offer can be revoked.

A question however arises whether a tenderer can revoke his tender inspite of a clear clause in the tender that the offer is kept open upto a particular date. Suppose a tenderer mentions in his offer that the offer is kept open for 3 months commencing from a particular date, but, he withdraws the tender before such 3 months period. Suppose the public body which has issued the NIT forfeits EMD relying upon a clause in the NIT to the effect that E.M.D. can be forfeited if the offer is withdrawn before the period of 3 months. It is submitted that such an action of the public body is not valid under law. Unless there is a separate consideration for the condition of not withdrawing the tender before a particular period, the tenderer is free withdraw his offer notwithstanding his promise not to withdraw the offer. (State of M.P. Vs Hakim Singh AIR 1983 M.P. 24).

If the offeror revokes his offer, such revocation is complete against him (the person who is revoking the offer), the moment he has put the letter of revocation in the course of transmission. However, as against the offeree, a revocation is complete when it comes to the actual knowledge of the offeree.
A proposal is deemed to be revoked under the following circumstances:
When a proposal is revoked by communication of notice of revocation.
By the lapse of time prescribed in the proposal (if no time prescribed, by lapse of a reasonable time).
When the proposal is rejected by the offeree.
A proposal is revoked by death or insanity of the offeror.

The acceptance of offer should be made by some overt act like communication of it through a messenger or through a letter or some other reasonable means of communication. A mere mental decision of the offeree regarding the acceptance of the offer does not conclude the contract. Normally, in the case of public sector undertakings, mode of communication of acceptance is generally specified in NIT.

The communication of acceptance is complete as against the offeror when it is put in a course of transmission to him. However it is complete as against the acceptor when it comes to the knowledge of the offeror.

Acceptance should be communicated within the time specified in the tender. If the acceptance is delayed, the tenderer has a choice whether to accept or not the delayed acceptance of the offeree. In fact, the delayed acceptance of the offeree will be treated as an offer and it is for the original tenderer to accept it or not. Suppose, there is an offer in which no time is prescribed for acceptance, it does not mean that the offer can be accepted at any time. It should be accepted within a reasonable time. What is 'reasonable time' is a question of fact and it depends on circumstances of the case.

The acceptance in order to be effective must be (a) Unconditional (b) must be complete (c) It must be given by a person or the authority competent to give acceptance (d) It must be addressed to the offeror or his authorised representative (e) It must be communicated in the manner prescribed in the proposal [or if no manner is prescribed, in a reasonable manner] (f) It must be made before the offer is lapsed, revoked or rejected.

An agreement requires consideration in order to be valid and binding. In case of contracts with public bodies, normally, there is no problem because price is always paid for the works to be performed by a contractor. The price agreed to be paid is the consideration for the works agreed to be performed by the contractor. Similarly, the works agreed to be performed is the consideration for the promise of price to be paid by the employer. However, question of consideration assumes importance in the cases of following nature.

Suppose there is a term in the NIT that a tender should be kept open for a particular period and that tender should be submitted along with some E.M.D. and that E.M.D. is liable to be forfeited if the tenderer revokes his tender. To suppose one of the tenderers  agrees to keep his offer open till a particular period and not to withdraw the tender before that particular period, but, contrary to the agreement of not withdrawing the offer before a particular period, he withdraws the offer. Suppose the employer forfeits E.M.D. in accordance with the terms contained in the NIT. The question is whether the action of the employer is valid in law? It is submitted that the agreement between the employer and the tenderer in terms of which tenderer has agreed not to revoke his tender is not supported by any consideration. If such an agreement is to be valid, there should be a separate consideration from the employer.

Consideration can be past act or present act or future act (it may be an act or abstaining from doing something). The law relating to past consideration is having only an academic importance and normally in contracts between public bodies and contractors consideration is always either present act or future act. Normally in works contracts, consideration in the form of price is given in several installments depending on completion of various stages of work. In purchase contract, a public body pays the price either in advance or after receipt of goods from supplier. In a sale contract, public body normally receives price in advance. However, there can be credit sales also.

Under law, consideration need not be adequate. However if the consideration is inadequate, it may give credence to the allegations of one of the parties that the contract has been procured by the other party under coercion or undue influence or misrepresentation or fraud.

If the consideration in the agreement is illegal, the agreement is void. Suppose A agrees to supply illicit liquor to B at a particular price. Later on, B pays the price but A has failed to supply the illicit liquor. B cannot file a suit against A for specific performance of the promise because the consideration for the promise of payment of money is supply of illicit liquor the supply of which is prohibited and visited with penal consequences.

Sometimes, the consideration of an agreement may be lawful but the object of the agreement may not be lawful. Suppose A agrees to lease out his house for B, and B wants to use the house for the purpose of trade in illicit liquor. A knows the purpose for which B has taken the house. Here, the contract is only for leasing the house and B is supplying consideration in the shape of rent. The consideration is lawful. But the object of the contract is not lawful. Hence, the agreement cannot be enforced.

The above issues are only having academic importance and have normally no place in contract of public bodies because very rarely public bodies enter into agreement, the consideration or the object of which is illegal. However, sometimes, a public body may do so in ignorance of law. In the knowledge of this author, there was a case of an agreement to sell a tiger by a public body to a private circus company. The public body owns a tiger on account of the zoo maintained by it and the authorities of the public body were not aware of the provisions of the Wild Life Act which prohibit the selling of wild animals. Selling of wild animals is an offence under the Act and hence the consideration of the agreement as well as the object of the agreement are illegal.
CAPACITY OF THE PARTIES TO THE CONTRACT:
The following categories of persons are not competent to enter into contract:
Minors (b) Insane persons (c) Persons in intoxicated state (d) Foreign rulers
(e) Ambassadors and envoys (f) Alien enemies (g) Bankrupts.

When contracts are entered into by a public body with partnership firms, it is necessary to verify registration of the firms. When a contract is entered into with a company, memorandum of association should be verified, so that the subject matter of the contract is not beyond the contractual capacity of the company.
CONSENT OF THE PARTIES TO THE CONTRACT:
An agreement is not enforceable if it is vitiated by any of the following (1) Mistake (2) Misrepresentation (3) Fraud (4) Coercion and (5) Undue influence.

Sometimes, in contracts with public bodies, contractors agitate that they were influenced by some misrepresentation made by the authorities of the public body. So, the authorities of the public body must be clear in the correspondence with the contractors. The allegations of coercion and undue influence are also made sometimes by contractors and there are cases where courts have accepted such allegations. Especially, some public bodies refuse to process bills unless an unconditional ‘no claim certificate’ is given by their contractors. If a contractor gives a ‘no claim certificate’ with some reservations, some public bodies refuse to process the bills. In such cases, the contractors give ‘no claim certificate’ initially and after receipt of the amount under the final bill, raise further claims stating that the no claim certificate was given under coercion. A public body should be very careful and it should be clearly mentioned in writing in correspondence with its contractors that they can claim the final bill with whatever exceptions and reservations they want to make. The public body also should decide at the time of processing the final bill itself whether it has any claims against the contractors for damages on account of delay or defective work.

In works contracts, the performance of work by a contractor is, sometimes dependent on the performance of some of the obligations on the part of the employer. Suppose, a contractor agrees to construct a building within two years from the date of entering into the contract and the employer agrees to supply steel and cement at a particular rate, at specified times. The contractor need not perform his part of the agreement unless the employer performed his obligations. The order of performance of reciprocal promises depends on the nature of the contract.

The contract should be performed at a reasonable time and at a reasonable place if no time and place of performance is fixed in the contract. Suppose, a public body orders for supply of medicines to its hospital. The period before which the supply is to be made is prescribed. But no time is prescribed i.e., at what hour the supply is to be made is not prescribed. Suppose the supplier brings medicines at 2 a.m. in the night, when none of the officials was present in the hospital to take delivery. It is submitted that such performance is not a valid performance because under law, supply must be made at a reasonable time. However, 'what is reasonable' is a question of fact. For instance, some of the items used in building construction like stones, bricks etc., are supplied during night time only by several contractors. The employer cannot refuse the performance in such cases. However, in the above illustration, if it is agreed that the stones and bricks required for building will be supplied only during day time, the contractor cannot insist that he would deliver at night time, even if the other similarly situated contractors usually supply such articles at night time.

The conditions as to reasonableness in performance of contract applies to place also. The delivery of material by the contractors should be made at a reasonable place if no specified place is prescribed. 'What is reasonable' is a question of fact and depends on the circumstances of the case.

Sometimes, contracts are divisible and some times not. If a contract is not divisible the promisee may refuse to accept the performance if the promisor performs a part of the promise. Suppose, there is an agreement for painting of a picture of a leader. The painter paints half of picture and then demands price for that portion expressing his inability for completing the remaining portion. It is submitted that the employer not only need not pay that price for the half work done by the promissor but also can claim damages against the painter for non-performance of the contract. On the other hand, where a contract is divisible, price must be paid for the part performance also. Eg.: Suppose a public body enters into a contract for purchase of 1000 tons of steel to be delivered at the rate of 100 tons a month. The contractor supplies 500 tons of steel within five months and expresses his inability for supply of the remaining quantity. Suppose the public body has already consumed the steel supplied to it. It is submitted that the contractor is entitled for pro-rata amount. Of course the public body is entitled for damages against the contractor for not supplying the remaining quantity. On the other hand, if the employer has not utilised the items already supplied to him and if the contractor was not ready and willing to perform the remaining part of the contract, the employer is entitled to reject the part-performance and the contractor should take back items already supplied. The employer is entitled for damages against the contractor for non-performance of the contract as originally agreed to.

A contract which is enforceable at the instance of one of the parties but not at the instance of the other party to the contract, is called as Voidable contract. If one of the parties enters into a contract on account of fraud, misrepresentation, coercion or undue influence on the part of the other party,  the first party is entitled either to enforce or to avoid the contract at its option.

If a person who is entitled to avoid the contract rescinds the same or when the contract is or becomes void, the party who has already received any benefit under the contract is bound to restore such benefit to the other party. These principles are laid down in section 64 and 65 of the Contract Act.

In most of the cases, public bodies do insist on firm price contract. However, if the parties enter into a supply or works contract and the items to be supplied or work to be executed involves such inputs like iron, steel and cement, the prices of which do normally increase every year, it is not possible for the parties to have a firm price contract. So in such contract there would be a price variation formula and the base prices of various items as on the date of contract are given in the contract. Sometimes disputes arise about price variation. Normally disputes arise on account of the difference in measurements of quantity of work done, or extra work done by the contractor which was not originally mentioned in the contract, but directed by the proper authority to execute the same; or change in the plans which changed the contract so substantially that the original rates are no longer workable. Whenever there is a dispute regarding price, the contractual terms regarding price variation have to be given effect to. If the terms of the contract are not applicable to the matter in dispute, the contractor is entitled for a reasonable rate. 'What is reasonable' is a question of fact and if a dispute arises, either a civil court or an Arbitrator will decide the same.

Where a contractor agrees to supply several articles and if he wants to claim excise duty as extra, he should mention this aspect in his tender very clearly. If he does not include this term in his tender, the prices quoted therein are presumed to include the element of excise duty also and he cannot claim the same separately. However, section 64(A) of the sale of Goods Act provides that even in the absence of stipulation in the contract providing for statutory variation in excise duty, a contractor is entitled to reimbursement of such additional amount as he is obliged to pay as a result of any increase or imposition taking place after making of the contract. However, if the increase or fresh imposition of excise duty relates to raw materials used in the finished goods agreed to be sold but not on the finished products, the contractor is not entitled for the benefit of section 64(A) of the Sale of Goods Act.

If there is an agreement between a contractor and public body whereby the contractor agrees to sell a particular product, the sales tax on such product is payable only by the contractor. The contractor cannot pass on to the purchaser unless the purchaser has agreed to bear the same. If a tenderer quotes a particular price without claiming sales tax extra, the presumption is that the price includes sales tax. However, if he quotes sales tax as extra, he is entitled for reimbursement of the sales tax, provided he is liable to be assessed and the transaction of sale legally attracts sales tax. The benefit of section 64(A) of Sales of Goods Act applies to Sales Tax also.

Where there is a long term contract between a contractor and a public body, for instance in a building or engineering contract, the contractor may become liable to pay wages to his labour more than the wages he was liable to pay as on the date of agreement between him and the public body on account of several reasons. The extra wages paid by the contractor to his employees cannot be claimed as a matter of right unless there is a clause in the contract permitting reimbursement of extra wages paid by the contractor. If there is no any agreement for the reimbursement of wage escalation, the contractor cannot claim extra wages paid to his workmen even if such extra wages are paid on account of the legislation which compels him to pay such wages.

Where there is a wage escalation clause, the clause should be strictly construed. If reimbursement is involved, the contractor is entitled for reimbursement only after he had shown the proof of payment of extra wages.
TIME IS THE ESSENCE OF THE CONTRACT:

In most of the contracts, parties mention that time for delivery or performance is the essence of contract. If one of the parties fail to deliver or perform the contract within the time allowed, the other party to the contract can terminate the contract and claim damages for non-performance of contract. However, one of the parties may accept delayed performance on the part of the other, either reserving a right to claim damages for delayed performance or may merely condone the delay.

Much case law is there on the above aspect. There are several decisions stating that ‘whether time is essence of contract or not’ is a matter to be decided by examining the real intention of the parties at the time of entering into the contract. A mere assertion in the contract that time is the essence of contract is not a conclusive proof to show that time is really the essence of contract. Normally, unless a clear contrary intention is manifested, in contracts involving immovable properties, time is not the essence of contract and in contracts involving supply of movable articles, time is the essence of contract. If in any contract it is proved that time is the essence of contract and one of the parties fails to perform his promise within the stipulated time, the other party can put an end to the contract reserving a right to claim damages for breach of contract. However, if one of the parties is agreeable to accept delayed performance, but wants to claim damages for delayed performance, he must do so by giving a notice to that effect at the time of extension of time for performance of contract. If such notice is not given at the time of extension of time to the other party, the party accepting the delayed

performance cannot subsequently claim damages. (Section 55 of the Contract Act). The contractors and the public bodies should be very clear about this aspect at the time of extension of time for performance of contract.

Section 39 of the Contract Act deals with Anticipatory Breach of Contract. Suppose a contractor agrees to supply some articles to a public body and much before the time for performance has arrived, he makes it clear that he will not perform the contract on the due date. It is advisable for the public body to accept breach of contract by the other party and to reserve a right to claim damages. If the public body refuses to accept the breach and waits till expiry of time for performance, the party expressing his inability to perform the contract can take advantage of any of the circumstances which would excuse his performance occurring between the date on which he expressed his inability and the normal date of performance of the contract. Let us take the following illustration.

'A' agreed to construct a building for a public body and deliver the possession of it within two years of the date of agreement. The date of agreement is 1st January, 1997. On 1st July, 1997 he informed the public body that he is not in a position to perform his promise and that he is putting an end to the contract. Inspite of such letter from ‘A’, the other party continued to request 'A' for completing the construction as originally agreed to. ‘A’ stopped the corresponding with the public body. On 30th July, 1998 the State Government issued a notification acquiring the land on which the building was to be constructed by ‘A’ (under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act). Immediately the public body issues a notice to ‘A' claiming damages for breach of contract on the ground that when the contractor committed the breach, the land was not acquired by the State Government. It is submitted that ‘A’ is entitled to take benefit of the notification by the Government and he is excused from the performance of the contract and he need not pay any damages. The position would be different if the public body accepts the repudiation of the contract by ‘A’ on 1st July, 1997 itself reserving the right to recover damages.
Under Section 72 of the Contract Act, if any money is paid to any person or any article is delivered to any person by mistake, he must repay or return it.

Section 62 of the contract provides that if the parties to the contract agreed to substitute a new contract in the place of old contract, the original contract need not be performed. If the obligation under the new contract is not performed by one of the parties, the other party can file a suit for specific performance or for damages only on the basis of the new contract. For instance, a contractor has agreed to supply a particular quantity and quality of steel before a particular date at an agreed price. Subsequently, the contractor expressed his inability to supply the steel of that particular quantity and quality and instead agreed to supply a different quality of steel of a different quantity for the same price. This new offer by the contractor has been agreed to by the other party to the contract. On the due date of performance, the contractor failed to perform the new promise. The other party can take legal proceeding only for enforcing the new contract. The other party cannot demand performance of their original promise by the contractor. Substitution of new promise in place of old promise is called "Novation of Contract". English law differs from the Indian law in this regard. In the above illustration, under the English law, legal proceedings can be instituted for performance of the original promise.

Suppose a public body enters into a contract for purchase of some articles from a contractor and the contractor agreed to supply the articles in several installments. Suppose the contractor commits breach of contract on account of his failure to supply the articles in some installments as per the agreement without any justifiable reason. The purchaser public body is entitled to terminate the contract. Various terms are used for termination of contract. It may be 'cancellation' of the contract; ‘electing to treat the contract at an end’; "recession" etc. If a contract has been terminated by one of the parties on account of breach of contract of the other party, the contract does not cease to exist; the following are its consequence:
The party who has committed the breach need not perform his obligation under the contract but he is liable to pay damages/compensate the victim for not receiving the promised performance.

Both the contracting parties are liable for rights and obligations which accrued before the termination, like liability for damages for losses caused by earlier breach and liability for payments earned under the contract. The party who has terminated the contract is entitled to claim the amount as already due from the other party before the termination.
The terms of a contract continue to apply. Damages will be assessed with reference to the terms of the contract and provisions like arbitration clauses will continue to apply.

If a public body enters into a contract with an outsider it has the obligation to give a notice for termination to the other party to remedy his breach if the contract is of such a nature that the breach can be remedied. Even otherwise where one of the contracting parties is a 'State' under Article 12 of the Constitution, no prejudicial action can be taken against the other contracting party unless an opportunity to show cause is given to the other party.

In case of late or delayed performance, where time is the essence of contract, the victim need not even inform the defaulting party that he is terminating the contract. He can simply refuse to accept the delayed performance when tendered. However, if there is a defective performance, the party which wishes to reject the defective performance, must do so by giving a specific notice. If time is not the essence of contract and the time mentioned in the contract has expired, the victim can make the time essence of contract by sending a notice for performance.
When a contract is entered into between the parties, it gets discharged in any of the following ways:
Performance of contract (2) Impossibility of performance (3) Breach of contract.

Provisions relating to performance are already discussed. Section 56 of the Contract Act deals with (a) contracts which are impossible (b) contracts where the parties have discovered that the performance of the contract was impossible even at the time of entering into contract which fact they were unaware of and            (c) contract which became impossible after the contract is entered into. The English Law of Frustration is not strictly applicable to India. In the case of Sathya Vrata Ghosh Vs Mungiram Bhangur and Company (1954 Supreme Court  journal 120), Supreme Court of India clarified that section 56 of the Contract Act is the complete law relating to all types of impossible contracts, and the English common Law principles of frustration would not apply in India. Impossibility of performance may be clear from the nature of agreement itself. For instance, 'A' agrees to cause rain on the next date of the agreement by using his magical powers. 'B' has agreed to pay some specific amount in consideration of the promise. This agreement is void because it is an agreement  to do an act which is impossible.

Suppose A agrees to give his house for rent to B which is situated at a place different from the place in which the agreement entered into. B has agreed to pay a specific rent. Unknown to both parties, the house was fully damaged due to an earthquake even at the time of entering into the agreement. This agreement is void because of impossibility of performance even though at the time of entering into contract parties were not aware impossibility of performance.

Suppose A agrees to supply some articles to a person residing in another country. Before the due date of performance a war broke out and the Governments of both the countries prohibited trade between both the counties. Here, the contract became void on account of subsequent event, i.e., prohibition by law. Hence, the contract became impossible and need not be performed.

Sometimes, a supervening event (an event occurred after the date of contract) may not make the performance of the contract impossible but it may change the nature of contract in such a way that to compel the parties to abide by the contractual obligation would cause serious injustice to one of the parties, and to compel performance of such contract would amount to compelling the parties to perform altogether a new contract. Look at the following case: Metropolitan Water Board Vs Dick Kerr and Company Ltd., (1918) Appeal Cases 119.

In this case, A agreed to supply cement to B at a particular rate for a particular period. However, after entering into contract, a war broke out and after war ended the prices of cement were increased so steeply that the promisor was no longer in a position to supply at the agreed rate. The court held that it is not a case of simple commercial loss arising out of normal market risk but it is arising out of some event which cannot be foreseen by the parties and that the event has changed the nature of contract to such an extent that it would be an injustice if the promisor is compelled to supply cement at the contractual rates.

A frustration of a contract leads to automatic termination of a contract and both the contracting parties are exempted from further performance of contract. Neither party would be liable to pay damages to the other party. However, if any one of the parties has received any benefit under the agreement he must restore the same or pay compensation for it to the other party.
Following are the main  remedies for breach of contract. (1) Damages
Specifics performance of contract; and (3) Injunction.
The Contract Act deals with principles relating to damages in Sections 73 and
74. Specific relief Act 1963 deals with Specific performance of Contract and injunction.

When a contract is entered into, the assumption is that both the parties would perform their respective obligations. A contract may provide for detailed provisions relating to time, manner, quantity, quality and place of performance. However, the possibility of one of the parties committing a breach cannot be ruled out. So, the Contract Act takes into consideration of such possibility and law is laid down regarding consequences of non-performance of contract and measurement of damages to be paid to the party which adversely suffers on account of non-performance.

When one of the parties commits a breach of contract, the other party is entitled for compensation for any loss caused to him;  or damages which  naturally arose in the course of things from such breach; or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of contract. Compensation or damages will not be given  for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of breach. A party who suffers on account of breach of contract should try to mitigate the loss caused to him. While awarding damages courts would examine whether a party who suffered consequences of breach of contract has utilised all the means which existed for remedying the inconvenience caused by non-performance.

The object of granting damages to the injured party on account of breach of contract is to place him in the same position as he would be if the contract has been performed by the other party instead of committing breach. In most of the cases, compensation through money may be sufficient and the Contract Act deals with only compensation or damages.

Section 73 of the Contract Act deals with the principle of granting damages. Damages occurring from ordinary and natural result of breach of contract would be granted to the party. For example, on 1st August, 2000 ‘A’ entered into agreement with ‘B’ to supply to B one hundred bags of rice of a particular quality at Rs.1,300/- per bag on 1st September, 2000. On the due date of performance, A did not supply the rice as promised. On 1st September, 2000 the market price was Rs.1,400/-  per bag. So, B is entitled for compensation at the rate of Rs.100/- per bag for 100 bags. The damages granted in this case are the ordinary damages naturally resulting from breach of contract. Both parties to the contract were aware of the possibility of the loss if the contract is not performed on the due date. In the illustration given above, ‘A’  is aware that if he does not supply rice as promised on 1st September, 2000 ‘B’ will be compelled to purchase it in the open market and that if ‘B’ is compelled pay a higher price, to that extent, ‘B’ will suffer loss. These damages are known as ordinary damages because they are not dependant upon any special circumstances with in the exclusive knowledge of the parties to the contract only.

‘A’ entered into contract with a transport company for transporting some articles to Delhi From Hyderabad for the purpose of selling those articles in an exhibition to be held at Delhi on 1st August, 2000. As per the contract the articles should reach Delhi on or before 30th July, 2000. ‘A’ has made it clear to the transport company his purpose of sending the goods to Delhi and the loss of profits for him if the goods do not reach Delhi before the due date. The transporter committed a breach of contract. In this case, ‘A’ is entitled not only for the ordinary damages for delay which are payable in case of delay in transportation, as per the custom of the trade but also for loss of profits towards special damages. Special damages are those damages occurring on account of special circumstances known to both the parties at the time of entering into contract itself. The promisor knows that the other party would suffer special loss if he commits a breach of contract.

In addition to ordinary and special damages, courts would also grant two other types damages known as (a) nominal damages (b) exemplary or punitive damages. Nominal damages are granted just to recognise the right of the party to receive damages but not for the purpose of compensating him from the loss. Suppose A agrees to supply B some articles for a particular price on 1st August, 2000. On the due date, A commits breach but B is able to procure the articles in the open market, at the same price without suffering any other loss on any account. In this case court would grant nominal damages to the party who suffered the breach, just to vindicate the legal rights of the party.

Exemplary or punitive damages are granted in order to punish the party who has committed breach of contract but not for compensating the victim of breach of contract. Suppose, a multimillionaire, a reputed businessman, who is having several lakhs of rupees in his current account in a particular bank issues a cheque for rupees one hundred and the officials of the bank dishonour the cheque on account of their negligence. The court would grant heavy damages to the party not just to compensate but to punish the person who has committed breach.

Section 74 of the Contract Act deals with liquidated damages and penalty. There are many leading cases on the subject of liquidated damages. Liquidated damages represent damages estimated by both the parties to the contract if either of the parties commits a breach of contract. The purpose of including a clause relating to liquidated damages is two-fold. Firstly, the nature of the contract may be such that if either of the parties commits a breach, actual quantification of damages would be very complicated and not an easy process. Secondly, both parties do not want a further dispute regarding methods of computing the loss and calculating the damages. Both parties would know at the time of entering into contract itself what would be the monetary consequence of breach of contract.

While the purpose of a clause relating to liquidated damages is to make both parties free from the problem relating to calculation of actual loss in case of breach of contract, in practice, it is seen that one of the contracting parties would usually resort to litigation, regarding quantum of damages.

Section 74 of the Contract Act is one of the most misunderstood sections not because the provisions contained therein are complicated but because of the tendency of several legal advisers to import English Law relating to liquidated damages and penalty into it for the purpose of interpretation. Sometimes, some judges too commit this error. In fact the law is very simple and is as follows:

If some amount is mentioned as damages (whether the parties call it as liquidated damages or penalty) in a contract, and if one of the parties is entitled to receive any compensation on account of breach of contract by the other party, he is entitled to receive a ‘reasonable compensation’ not exceeding the amount mentioned in the contract towards damages (either under the leading ‘Liquidated damages or penalty’).

What the party entitled is reasonable compensation only not exceeding the sum mentioned as damages in the contract. Sometimes, the court may agree that the pre-estimated damages represent reasonable compensation in a particular case. The party who suffers breach is dispensed with proof relating to actual quantum of damages or actual loss even though he has to establish that he suffered loss. However, courts are not free from the responsibility of arriving at reasonable compensation. If a dispute arises between the parties, the party entitled for damages should prove that reasonable compensation in that particular case is not less than the liquidated damages. The other party, if it wants to escape from paying liquidated damages, should prove that the reasonable compensation entitled by the other party is much less than the liquidated damages.

Strictly speaking, it is unnecessary to include any stipulations by way of penalty in a contract because, in view of Section 74 of Contract, only reasonable compensation will be paid. However, due to the influence of English Law, in many of the contracts involving public bodies clauses are inserted stipulating for penalties in case of breach of contract. However, there is no actual necessity of doing away with penalty clauses if the public body feels that they will have a deterrent effect on the contractors.
Forfeiture clauses frequently come up before the courts in India. Some of the leading cases, decided by the Supreme Court on forfeiture clauses are following:
Fatch Chand Vs Balkishan Das, AIR 1963 S.C. 1955
Maula Bux Vs Union of India, AIR 1970 S.C. 1955
Shri Hanuman Cotton Mills Vs Tata Aircraft Ltd., AIR 1970 S.C. 1986
Union of India Vs Rajpur Distillery and Chemical Company Ltd., AIR 1973 S.C. 1098
State of Maharastra Vs D.B.Kulkarni (1979) 2 S.C.C. 217.

Inspite of number of judgements relating to forfeiture clauses, law is not explained in a clear language. However, it can be said that if the amount to be forfeited is 'earnest money', the forfeiture clause is legally valid. But, if the amount to be forfeited is a 'security deposit', forfeiture clause is not valid.

Ultimately, whether a clause relating to liquidated damages or forfeiture will be upheld or not depends upon the facts of each case. The expression used by the parties is not conclusive. If the sum mentioned as liquidated damages is extravagant and unconscionable in amount, in comparison with greatest loss that could conceivably be proved to have occurred from breach, it will be treated as penalty and hence, unreasonable.

Sometimes, a contract between the parties may itself narrate the circumstances, the existence of which will excuse non-performance of the contract in part or in full. These clauses are called Force Majeure clauses.
If the parties clearly mention various circumstances which will excuse the performance, the problem will be lessened. The following clauses merit our discussion.

WAR: If war breaks out and the performance of contract is affected on account of it, it is one of the excuses. However, mere imposing restrictions and consequent difficulty in delivery of articles at contracted prices is not excused.

DIFFICULTY IN SUPPLIES: Failure of crop due to reasons of nature which could reasonably be anticipated, though rare, is not a force majeure. However, natural calamities like typhoons which are very rare excuse the performance of contract.

ROUTE CLOSURE: Suppose, there is a contract, the performance of which is possible only if a particular route is opened. If that route is closed, for any reason, it is a force majeure. However, if there are number of routes, even if the usual route is closed, the contract must be performed by the parties.

THIRD PARTY FAILURE: Suppose A enters into contract with B for supply of certain quantity of cement at a particular price. A relied upon supplies from C to him as per the contract between A & C. On account of a force majeure event C could not supply cement to A and consequently A could not supply cement to B. In a suit filed by B against A, the failure of contract between A & C cannot be a force majeure event, because in the contract between A & B there is no reference to A and C.

VIS MAJEURE: The above expression covers acts of enemies of State as well as acts of God. For non-believers in God, this expression should be taken as unusual acts of nature, not in contemplation of the parties at the time of entering into contract like earthquakes, lightening, typhoon etc.

UNFORESEEN CIRCUMSTANCES: If the force majeure clause includes an expression - 'Unforeseen Circumstances' as excusing performance of contract, it leads to a lot of controversy between the parties. It is better to avoid such expression in the force majeure clause. If one of the parties is prevented by performance of contract due to unforeseen circumstances beyond his control the law will take its own course and if the court comes to conclusion that it became impossible for him to perform the contract, he will be excused under Section 56 of Contract Act. So special mention of 'Unforeseen Circumstances' is not necessary.

In most of the contracts, public bodies insist on performance guarantees by the contractors. Contractors do generally give bank guarantees for performance of their obligation under the contract. Bank guarantees usually contain a clause that mere demand by the promisee stating that the promisor has committed breach of contract is a sufficient proof of breach and that the Bank would pay the sum guaranteed without any protest. In several cases, the Supreme Court held that the unconditional bank guarantees are independent of the contracts between the principle debtor and the original promisee, and that the banks should honour their guarantees without any protest if there is a mere demand unless there is any fraud. Inspite of unambiguous law laid down by the Supreme Court, several lower courts grant stay on guarantees indiscriminately thus causing loss of faith in the legal system. It is observed that in most of the cases injunctions are granted by trial courts on account of ignorance of law laid down by the Supreme Court.

If one of the parties commits a breach of contract remedy is not just claiming damages only always. In appropriate cases, courts do grant specific performance of the contract. In such cases where the loss suffered by the party on account of breach of contract cannot be compensated by payment of money, usually specific performance is granted. For instance, A agrees to sell a piece of land to B. If A commits breach of contract, B can get an order from the court in his favour, directing A to sell the land as per the agreement.

Suppose, A  agrees to sell a piece of land to B. After sometime, B comes to know that A has executed another agreement in favour of C to sell the same piece of land. B can  approach a competent court for a direction restraining from selling the agreed piece of land to C. The direction given by the court is known as injunction. Injunctions could be either prohibitory or mandatory.
The remedies of specific performance and injunction are given under Specific Relief Act.

'AB' a Government Company at Delhi engaged in trade of some items deputed its Managing Director to Mumbai for negotiation and finalisation of a commercial deal worth 10 crores with a leading private company. The Managing Director boarded flight at Delhi on 1st September, 2000 at 7 AM and reached Mumbai Airport by 9 AM on the same date. From Airport he engaged a taxi and checked in a five star hotel located near Churchgate area. He got appointment with the President of the private company by 4PM on the date. By 3PM, when he was about to leave the hotel he realised that he lost one of the small brief cases he was carrying with him which contained all the important documents relating to the business deal. Immediately, he contacted the President of the private company and got postponed his meeting to 5th September, 2000. On the evening of1st September, 2000 itself he went to the office of "Times of India" and got published an advertisement in the newspaper dated 2.9.2000 to the following effect.

"I lost a brief case containing cash of Rs.25000/- and important documents pertaining to "AB" Company on 1st September, 2000 while travelling from Delhi to Bombay. Finder may send the same to the following address. He will be rewarded with Rs.10000/-".

On the night of 2nd September the Managing Director received in his hotel room a parcel containing the brief case through a private courier. The documents and cash were intact. There was a covering letter from one "X", the taxi driver who drove the Managing Director from Mumbai Airport to the Hotel. While the Managing Director was going through the letter, 'X' entered into the room and introduced himself as the person who sent the courier. The Managing Director recognised him as the taxi driver and repeatedly thanked him for the help rendered by him. He praised the honesty of the driver who did not yield to the temptation of misappropriating the cash. After a few minutes, the MD wanted to pay the courier charges and asked him to show the receipt given by the courier agency. Receipt dated 1.9.2000 issued by the courier for Rs.200/- was shown by the taxi driver. MD asked the driver whether all the entries in the receipt are true and the driver replied in affirmative. Then the driver was offered Rs.200/- by MD. The taxi driver claimed the reward of Rs.10000/- offered by the Managing Director through the newspaper. Managing Director refused to pay. Later on MD could clinch a successful deal with the private company.

On 15th October, 2000 'X' filed a suit against the Managing Director claiming Rs.10000/- with interest. His suit was decreed in the trial court. MD filed appeal in the District Court and the decree was set aside. The driver approached the High Court unsuccessfully. The matter came to the Supreme Court through SLP. Decide?

"AB" & Co., a Government company located at Dhanbad (hereinafter  referred to as the Government company) engaged in production and sale of cooking coal of a particular quality was finding it difficult to sell its products at the price fixed by it. The price fixed by the Government company was Rs.1100/- per unit for orders below 10000 units and Rs.1000/- per unit for orders above 10000 units. On one day, i.e., on 10th September, 2000, the Government company received a letter dated 6th September, 2000, posted on the same date, from a private company at Hyderabad to the following effect.

"We offer to purchase 50000 units of cooking coal from you at the price fixed by you which we came to know as Rs.1000/- per unit. We need delivery of the material latest by 25th September at our godown at Hyderabad. Please load the material by 'X' transport agency on or before 15th September, at Dhanbad so as to reach Hyderabad latest by 25th September".

The General Manager (Marketing) of the Government company who received the above letter immediately called the Deputy General Manager (Marketing) and asked him to make arrangements for delivery of material to the private company. The letter was a great relief to the General Manager as they could get an order worth 5 crores at a time when the market conditions were not favourable. The DGM informed the GM about his efforts in securing the order. He showed copy of the Regd. post Ack. Due letter issued by him to the private company at Hyderabad on 3rd September, 2000 when GM was on tour. The letter reads as follows.

"Please refer your telephonic enquiry regarding our price for 50000 units of cooking coal. The undersigned quoted the prices through telephone. We have not heard anything  from you. This is to put on record the quotation given by us through telephone. We offer to sell 50000 units of coal to you at the rate of Rs.1000/- per unit. We came to know that you need material latest by
25th September, 2000. We will load the same by 15th September. We prefer to sent the material by 'X' transport agency.
Looking for mutually profitable business deals                Yours faithfully,
DGM showed the GM the acknowledgement received from the private company. The authorised official of the private company at Hyderabad signed on the acknowledgement on 7th September, 2000.
On 14th September the Government company received a telegram from the private company at Hyderabad to the following effect.
"We cancel our order sent to you vide out letter dated 6th September, 2000".

GM and DGM of the Government company were very much frustrated. On discrete enquiries, they came to know that another Government company located near Hyderabad offered the private company coal at Rs.1050/- per unit and the private company preferred the said offer because the overall cost was lower on account of lower transport cost.

The Government company at Dhanbad had to sell the material, which was identified for the private company at Hyderabad, in the open market for Rs.950/- per unit thus incurring loss of Rs.25 lakhs. The Government company filed a suit against the private company for recovery of Rs.25 lakhs. It won in Dhanbad Civil Court but in Patna High Court the private company could get the judgement reversed. The Government company filed appeal in Supreme Court. Will it succeed. Give reasons for your decision.

A Ranchi based public sector company (hereinafter referred to as the Government company) engaged in manufacture of iron & steel is maintaining a hospital for its employees at it mines and it intended to ensure uninterrupted supply of medicines for a period of five years. On 1st July 2000, the company issued a notice inviting tenders (NIT) form reputed Chemists & Druggists for some specific drugs including a combination of anti-tubercular drug (which is a combination of Rifampicin 450mg plus Isoniazid 300mg). 10 firms submitted tenders out of which 2 firms were selected by the Government Company. One of the firms was located at Mumbai and the other was at Bangalore. The firm at Mumbai offered to supply but expressed its ability to supply only upto 20000 strips of 10 capsules each. Irrespective of the quantity supplied rate was Rs.63 per strip. The firm at Bangalore expressed its ability to supply only upto 5000 strips at the rate of Rs.57 per strip. The Government Company needs 15000 strips of the said drug.
On 1st August, 2000 the Chief Medical Officer (CMO) of the Government Company sent a letter through a messenger to the GM (Mktg.) of Mumbai firm as follows.

"We request you to supply 10000 strips of the anti-tubercular drug (Rifampicin 450mg + Isoniazid 300mg) at the price quoted by you. Delivery date will be informed to you shortly. Please sent your acceptance letter by post".

The GM (Mktg.) of Mumbai firm posted a letter on 2nd August, 2000 accepting the offer of the Government Company. This letter reached the Government Company on 4th August, 2000. Meanwhile on 3rd August, 2000 the GM (Mktg.) of Bangalore firm issued a fax message to the Government Company as follows.

"Please refer to our earlier quotation. Now we are in a position to supply up to 20000 strips at the rates quoted by us". The above fax message was seen by the CMO of the Government Company on 3rd August, 2000 itself and immediately a reply fax message was sent to the Bangalore firm requesting the said firm to supply 15000 strips at the prices quoted by them. On 3rd August, 2000 itself the CMO of the Government Company sent a fax message to GM (Mktg.) of the Mumbai firm as follows.

"We withdraw our order dated 1st August, 2000. We thank you for your quotation and we hope to have business dealings with you in future". The above fax message was personally received by the GM (Mktg.) of the Mumbai firm on 3rd August, 2000.

The Government Company purchased the entire required stock from the Bangalore firm. The Mumbai firm later on sold the stock of 10000 strips of the drug (which was to be sold to the Government Company) in the open market at the rate of Rs.60 per strip. The Mumbai firm filed a suit against the Government Company for recovering the loss of Rs.30000/-. Will it succeed? Give reasons.

A public sector company based at Dehradun (hereinafter referred to as the Government Company) is engaged in manufacturing, among others, industrial gas. Its sells industrial gas cylinders of a particular quantity at the rate of Rs.175/- per cylinder.
A private firm at Hyderabad (hereinafter referred to as 'the firm') issued a letter dt.11-8-2000 posted on the same date to the Government Company as follows.
"We intend to purchase 5000 cylinders from your company at the rate of Rs.175/- per cylinder. Please issue your acceptance letter through post".

The above letter was signed by the managing partner of the firm and addressed to the GM (sales) of the Government Company. The letter reached the PS to GM (Sales) of the Government Company on 16-8-2000 at 9AM. On          17-8-2000 at 10 AM the GM (Sales) of the Government Company has seen the letter of the firm and posted a letter of reply as follows.
"We accept your offer please let us know the time and place of delivery".

Before receipt of the above letter by the firm another company named 'AB' gave quotation for gas cylinders to the firm at Rs.155 per cylinder and hence on 14-8-2000 the managing partner of the firm issued a telegram to the Government Company runs as follows.
"We withdraw our offer of purchase of industrial gas cylinders contained in our letter dt.11-8-2000. We received a better quotation”.

The above telegram reached the Government Company on 15-8-2000 but on account of holiday for the office, it was served on the private secretary to GM (Sales) on 16-8-2000 at 9.30 AM. GM (Sales) was on tour on 16-8-2000. On     17-8-2000 private secretary to GM (Sales) was on leave and he kept all the letters on the table of GM but kept the telegram locked in the cupboard. GM (Sales) attended the office on 17-8-2000. As already stated, on 17-8-2000 he posted letter of acceptance to the letter dt.11-8-2000 issued by the firm. He did not see the telegram as it was kept in the locked cupboard by the private secretary. GM (Sales) read the telegram of the firm only on 18-8-2000 at 9 AM. Meanwhile on 16-8-2000 the firm received a telegram from 'AB' company as follows.

"We are sorry to inform you that our representative quoted the rates for the industrial gas cylinder at Rs.155 per cylinder by mistake. The said rate is for cooking gas cylinder. Our rate for industrial gas cylinder is Rs.185 per cylinder".
Immediately on receipt of the above telegram the firm sent a telegram dt.16-8-2000 to the GM (Sales) of the Government Company as follows.
"Please refer to our telegram dt.14-8-2000 withdrawing our offer letter dt.11-8-2000. We now withdraw  our telegram dt.14-8-2000".

GM (Sales) of the Government company received the telegram dated       16-8-2000 of the firm at 10 AM on 18-8-2000. He did not like the behaviour of the firm. Immediately he issued a telegram at 11AM on 18-8-2000 withdrawing his acceptance letter dt.17-8-2000.

At around 12 noon on 18-8-2000 the Managing Partner of the firm telephoned to GM (Sales) of the Government to enquire into the matter. GM (Sales) informed him that the acceptance letter as well as telegram withdrawing the acceptance letter had already been issued. The Managing partner pleaded for reconsideration of the matter to which GM (Sales) answered that he would think over about it. As the managing partner could not get any instant positive response from GM (Sales) of the Government Company, he also talked to 'AB' company about the price without any positive response.

On reconsideration of the matter, GM (Sales) of the Government company issued a fax message at 9 AM on 20-8-2000 (which was received and seen by the managing partner of the firm at 9 AM on 20-8-2000 itself) which reads as follows.
"We withdraw our telegram dt.18-8-2000 withdrawing our letter of acceptance dt.17-8-2000".

On 21-8-2000 MD of the Government company came to know of this transaction and advised GM (Sales) not to have any business dealing with the firm. The telegram of GM (Sales) of the Government company withdrawing letter of acceptance reached at 12 noon on 20-8-2000 and was immediately seen by the Managing Partner of the firm. Later, on 21-8-2000 the letter of acceptance dated 17-8-2000 reached the firm.

The Government company did not sell the material to the firm. The firm purchased the material from 'AB' company at the rate of Rs.185 per cylinder and sued the Government company for Rs.50,000/-. Will the firm succeed?

A public sector coal company was supplying coal to a public sector steel company, during 1st April, 1999 to 31st March, 2000 at a particular price per MT of coal. On 2nd April, 2000 the General Manager (purchase) of the Steel Company issued a letter to the General Manager (Sales) of the coal company as follows.

"We request you to supply 10000 MT of coal during the financial            year 2000 - 2001 also at the same rate at which you were supplying it during    1999 –2000. We require the entire stock at once to be delivered to us on or before 31st May, 2000.
There will not be any other formal order on you. Please communicate your acceptance by post".
The GM (Sales) of the coal company posted the acceptance letter on

10-4-2000 duly stamping and correctly addressing it to GM (purchase) of the steel company. However the letter is lost in transit. GM (p) of the steel company waited for the reply for a long time. Meanwhile price of coal has fallen and the steel company purchased the coal from the open market on 25th May 2000 coal stock sent by the coal company reached the steel company. GM (P) of the Steel Company refused to take delivery and the coal was returned to the coal company.
The coal company had to sell the coal in open market for a lesser price and it sued the steel company for the loss it incurred as well as the transport charges. Will it succeed?

A public sector oil company was in the process of overhauling the furniture, fixtures and other office items in their administrative office. One 'X' representing himself to be a computer hardware engineer entered into a computer service contract with the company and took possession of 20 numbers of computers to be serviced at his workshop and delivered to the company. The company asked for some security at the time of handing over the computers. He gave a promissory note for Rs.10 lakhs towards security on the condition that the note would be returned to him after the computers are delivered after service and if the computers are not returned by him the company can fall back upon the promissory note. He is a well known person in the town and a very rich person.

'X' is 6 ft. 2 inches tall, stout with mustache and looks to be aged around 22-23 years. However he was aged only 17 years on the date of issuing the promissory note to the company but he represented to the company that he was 23 years old computer engineer qualified from one of the Indian Institutes of Technology. The company believed him and entrusted the computers.
After taking possession of computers he sold them to another party who could not be traced. With the money realised from the sale of computers he purchased a Benz car worth 10 lakhs.
The company filed a suit against 'X'. Answer the following questions.

Whether the company can recover on the basis of pronote on the ground that he falsely misrepresented his age to be 23 years and that he should not allowed to plead in the court that he was only a minor on the date of execution of pronote.
Whether the company can get a direction from the court to 'X' to hand-over the Benz car to the company.

If the car is sold and the proceeds are spent by the minor, can the company get a direction from the court to compel the minor to repay money on the ground that he is otherwise rich and that he should not be allowed to take advantage of his own false statement.

A public sector television manufacturing company (a Government Company) appointed several dealers for sale of its  colour T.V. sets throughout the country. One 'XY' company was the main dealer for Kanpur city. 'XY' was given a right to appoint sub-dealers throughout the city.

As per the agreement between the Government Company and 'XY' company, T.V. sets should not be sold by 'XY' company to any user customer for an amount less than 11,950/- for each remote set and 11,000/- for each non-remote set. If 'XY' company appoints sub-dealers, a condition should be imposed that the T.V. sets should not be sold to user - customers by the sub-dealers below the price mentioned above and that if the sub-dealers violate the condition they would pay damages at the rate of Rs.500/- per set to the Government company.

'XY' company appointed 'AB' company as its sub-dealers for a particular region. As per the agreement between 'XY' and 'AB', the later company would not sell remote TV set below Rs.11,950/-  and non remote set below Rs.11,000/- and if it sells the sets below that price, for each set sold in that way it would pay Rs.500/- per set to the Government Company. A copy of the agreement between 'XY' and 'AB' was sent by 'XY' to the Government company at the request of the Government company after one month of the agreement.

After a few months after the agreement between 'XY' and 'AB', a few foreign TV brands entered the market with consumer attractive schemes and it became very difficult for 'AB' to sell the TVs at the price agreed with 'XY'. 'AB' started selling remote sets at the rate of Rs.10,000/-. They sold 100 TV sets at those prices.

The Government Company came to know about the price reduction offered by 'AB' company to the customers in the markets. The GM (Sales) of the Government Company issued notice to XY company demanding XY company to pay damages of Rs.50,000/- (500 x 100) because the sub-dealer appointed by 'XY' violated the condition. 'XY' company has not issued any reply. Similar notice was issued to 'AB' company also but no reply has been received.

The Government company filed a suit against XY company and AB company for recovery of Rs.50,000/- towards damages.
