The Government company contended that it can recover the damages either from XY company or from 'AB' company or jointly from both the companies. Both 'XY' and AB companies pleaded that they are not liable to pay any amount to the Government Company.

A Government company engaged in the business of execution of large civil engineering projects entered into a contract with a big private firm for execution of a project costing Rs.50 crores. The project was successfully completed but disputes arose between the Government Company and the private firm. There was no arbitration clause in the contract between the Government company and the firm. The Government company claims Rs.5 crores towards damages from the private firm for the loss caused to it on account of breach of conditions of the contract on the part of the private firm. The private firm, on the other hand claimed Rs.3 crores as damages against the Government company for the delay in execution of project. Each party attributed the responsibility for delay on the other.

The Government Company filed a civil suit against the private firm in the civil court at Delhi claiming Rs.5 crores. The private firm made a counter claim of Rs.3 crores. The issues were framed and the matter came up for trial.

When the  contract was in execution stage, one 'A' was the chief engineer in the Government company and 'B' was the Additional Chief Engineer. Both of them were closely associated with the execution of contract. They are now retired and both of them settled in Chennai. Their evidence is absolutely essential for the Government Company for success in the suit and for successfully defending the counter claim of the party.

The Government Company cited both 'A' and 'B' as witnesses. The advocate for company prayed the court for issuing summons to both these persons and accordingly court issued witness summons to both of them. The summons were duly served on them on 1-9-2000. They have to attend the court on             25th September, 2000.

As per the rules of the Government Company, retired employees who are required to give evidence on behalf of the company, would be treated on par with serving employees and would be extended all the tour benefits of TA, DA and accommodation. 'A' and 'B' are eligible for 4 star hotel stay, to and fro flight charges by economy class, taxi charges for local travel and Rs.250 per day towards DA.

On receiving summons, both 'A' and 'B' have written letters dt.2-9-2000 to the Government company that would like to give evidence in court only if they were paid flight charges in executive class without insisting on proof of travel, stay in a 5 star hotel, TA and DA local travel as per the company rules. Further they demanded cash of Rs.50,000/- each.

The evidence of 'A' and 'B' is absolutely essential for the Government company. Initially the Director (personnel) of the Government company tried to convince 'A' and 'B' that as the company is in the public sector, it cannot justify making any extra payment and providing extra facilities other than those mentioned in the TA rules. 'A' and 'B' refused to give evidence unless their terms are agreed to. Finally the Director (P) of the Government company thought that it is commercially prudent for the company to agree to the terms of 'A' and 'B' and after taking concurrence of the Managing Director, he issued identical letters to both A and B, the main portion of which is extracted below:

"Please refer to your letter dt.2-9-2000. Our company unconditionally accepts all the terms and conditions mentioned in your letter for giving evidence in the court. We will reimburse your hotel bills, travel expenses etc., as desired by you and you may prefer the bills after the evidence is over. Amount of 50,000/- demanded by you will be paid on or before 5th October, 2000”.

After receipt of the letters, 'A' and 'B' insisted that there should be a separate contract on proper stamp paper and accordingly contracts dt.15-9-2000 were entered into incorporating the contents of the above letter in the contracts. On behalf of the company the Managing Director signed the contracts.

Both 'A' and 'B' adduced evidence in the court on 25th September, 2000 and they claimed the amounts as per the contract. The company won the case in the court and got Rs.5 crores  from the firm. The Director (P) of the company put up a note to MD recomending payment to A & B and MD has sanctioned the necessary amount and forwarded the note to the chairman of the company for information. The chairman returned the note with the following remark; "Don't pay. The company cannot be taken for a ride by the retired employees". Accordingly the amount was not paid.

'A' and 'B' filed suits against the company on the basis of contracts dated 15-9-2000. They succeeded in the lower court and the company approached the High Court unsuccessfully. The company filed SLP in Supreme Court. Will it succeed?

In a Government company engaged in manufacturing and sale of iron and steel products, members of the public other than the State and Central Governments are holding 40% of shares. There are large numbers of share holders and it has decided to hold the Annual General Meeting (AGM) on 10th August 2000, in a particular city.

The company secretary favoured a bigger venue than the multipurpose hall of the company where the earlier AGMs were used to be conducted. On 1-8-2000, the company entered into a contract with 'X', a large AC theatre owner in the city, for that purpose. Rent for one day on 10-8-2000 was fixed as Rs.20,000/-. The purpose for which the theatre was hired was made known to he theatre owner.

The company paid advance of RS.10,000/- to 'X' on the date of the contract and the remaining amount is to be paid after the meeting is over. Preparations for the meeting were completed. The theatre owner announced stoppage of screening of films for 10-8-2000.

On 9-8-2000 communal riots broke out in the city and the Superintendent of Police imposed curfew in the city. All the meetings, conferences, cinema shows in the city were banned on 10-8-2000. This proclamation was made at        7 AM on 10-8-2000. AGM of the company could not take place.

The company demanded the theatre owner to refund Rs.10,000/- advance paid by it. The theatre owner refused to refund the amount. On the other hand, he demanded the company to pay the balance contract amount of Rs.10,000/-. A claim and counter claim were made in the court. Who will succeed? Give reasons.

Administrative office of a particular Government company was located in a rented premises at Mumbai. The owner of the premises lives in Bangalore. The company could get the premises for rent 20 years back. At present the financial position of the company is not sound. It is not in a position to shift to another premises due to non-availability of any accommodation for the rent the company was willing to pay.

On 10-3-2000 the company received a notice demanding payment of property tax in respect of the building in which the company is located. The amount is Rs.50,000/- for the year 1998-99. The last date of payment was           10-4-2000. The notice was addressed to the owner of the building but served on the MD of the company.
The company issued a letter dt.15-3-2000 to the owner of the building enclosing the tax notice and demanding him to pay the money. The owner issued a reply letter dt.20-3-2000 which reads as follows.

"I am not liable to pay the tax". On 25-3-2000 the company issued another letter to the owner requesting him to explain the reason why he was not liable to pay the property tax when he owns the property. There was no any reply. Two reminders were sent but there was no any reply. When contacted telephonically, he replied that he would not like to tell the reason to anybody.

On 30-4-2000 Municipal authorities attached the premises in question after completing prior legal requirements. Immediately a decision was taken by the company to pay the tax amount so that it can remain in possession. The tax amount was paid by the company.

The owner was demanded by the company to reimburse the tax amount of Rs.50,000/-. He replied that he never asked the company to pay the tax amount. Further, he added, that left to himself he would not pay the tax and allow the law to take its own course.
The company filed a suit for recovery of Rs.50,000/-. Will it succeed?

On 1st September, 2000 'A' contracts to sell 100 bags of sugar at Rs.2,000/- per bag to 'B' to be delivered on 15th September. Before 15th September,     ‘B’ entered into a contract with C for sale of 100 bags of sugar at the rate of 2,400/- per bag to be delivered on 30th September of that year. On 15th September, A committed breach of contract. Consequently B could not sell the sugar to C and suffered loss of profit. On 15th September, the market price of the sugar of the particular quality was RS.2,200 per bag. ‘B’ filed a suit against ‘A’ for damages for loss of profit of Rs.40,000/- Decide the entitlement of damages for B.

"A" at Chennai delivers to a transport company a machine on 1st August, 2000 year with a specific instruction to deliver that machine at the mill of 'A' located in Mumbai on or before 10th August, 2000. The transport company agreed to do so. In the transport trade the normal damages for the late delivery of such articles was Rs.500/- per day. 'A' informed the transport company that if the machine is not delivered on or before 10th August the mill which is already stopped cannot be restarted and that 'A' would suffer loss of average profit to Rs.10,000/- a day.

The transport company could deliver the machine only on 21st August, 2000. Similar machine was not available for purchase in India and it would take a minimum period of 2 months for import of such a machine.

On 11th August, 2000 Government of India enquired whether "A" could supply with in two days some product manufactured by him which was not manufactured by any other person in India. "A" could not enter to contract with Government of India because his mill could not be restarted on account of non delivery of machine by the transport company on 10th August. Due to loss of Government contract "A" suffered loss of estimated profit of Rs.1,00,000/-.
A filed a suit against the transport company claiming total damages of Rupees Two lakhs on two counts:
For loss of general profits for 10 days at the rate of Rs.10,000/- a day and
For loss of profit of Rs.1,00,000/- on account of loss of Government contract. The transport company is prepared to pay only 5000/- towards damages.

A contracts to sell and deliver to B on 1st January certain cloth with which he intends to manufacture caps of particular kind, for which there is no demand except at the season. B is expected to make a profit of Rs.50,000/- by making and selling caps. A has not delivered the cloth on the appointed day and delivered it too late to use it for making caps during the  season for that year. The contract price of the cloth was 2,50,000/-. On 1st January market price of cloth was 2,75,000/-. B  spent an amount of Rs.5,000/- towards expenses for preparation for manufacture of caps.
‘B’ sued ‘A’ for Rs.80,000/- towards damages under the following 3 heads:
difference between contract price and market price of the cloth Rs.25,000/-
loss of profit of Rs.50,000/- on account of non making and selling caps for the season.
expense for preparation for manufacture Rs.5,000/-.

A contract for supply of timber to a public sector company contained a clause than if the contractor commits breach of contract, the company was entitled for fixed damages of one lakh. It was specifically agreed that this amount should be treated as ‘liquidated’ damages. The contractor failed to supply. But the company did not suffer actual loss. The company filed a suit against the contractor for recovery of Rs.1,00,000/-. Will the company succeed?

A Government company entered into two contracts with a builder for construction of 24 nos. of quarters for its staff. Period of completion of contract was 2 years from the date of the execution of contract.
If the contractor commits a breach of contract, liquidated damages of Rs.5

.lakhs have to be paid in each contract. There was breach of contract by the contractor in both the contracts. In the first contract, the company actually suffered loss of only one lakh and any reasonable person could have estimated only that much of loss. In the second contract actual loss was Rs.9 lakhs. But the company claimed damages of 5 lakhs in each contract. The contractor declined to pay any amount. Decide the entitlement?

M/s. GP Company (GP) located at Ahmedabad had, by a message communicated by telephone offered to purchase cotton seed cake from BG Company (BG) located at Khamgoan. BG Company which received the phone call at Khamgoan instantaneously accepted the offer of GP Company and agreed to supply the required quantity. When BG Company failed to supply the material as promised, GP Company filed a suit in Ahmedabad for damages. BG Company contended that acceptance was complete in Khamgoan and hence contract was formed in Khamgoan and hence Ahmedabad court has no jurisdiction to try the suit. On the other hand GP Company contended that when telephone is used as medium of communication, acceptance is deemed to have been completed when the communication of acceptance is received by the proposer and in the instant case the proposer received telephonic message of acceptance at Ahmedabad and hence Ahmedabad court has jurisdiction. The trial court has accepted the contention of GP Company. The High court confirmed the order. BG Company filed SLP, in supreme court. The principal question before the Supreme Court is what is the place of the completion of contract in the instant case. As acceptance completes the contract, what is the place of acceptance, if telephone is used as a medium of communication, especially when both the parties clearly heard the communication of each other?
In the instant case, whether the acceptance is complete at Khamgoan or at Ahmedabad? Decide.

'A' is a Government Company engaged in manufacturing and sale of iron and steel products. 'B', a company in private sector wanted to purchase steel from A and issued a fax message on 1-8-2000 follows:
'Will you sell us 1000 tons of steel to us. Fax the lowest cash price'.
'A' sent a reply fax on 4/8/2000 as follows:
'Lowest cash price for steel is Rs.11,000/- per ton'.
'We agree to purchase 1000 tons of steel at Rs.11,000 per ton. We shall pay     and take delivery from your site on 9/8/2000.
When the authorised representative of 'B' went to the premises of 'A' with cash, the representative of 'A' refused to sell the stock.
'B' had to purchase the material from another company at the rate of Rs.12,000 per ton and hence filed a suit in the trial court for damages of Rs.10 lakhs.
The trial court decreed his suit. The High Court reversed the trial court judgement. Ultimately the matter came up before the Supreme Court. Decide.
A large public sector manufacturing company employing about 40,000 personnel inserted, inter alia, a clause in their rules to the following effect.

"The employment of a permanent employee shall be subject to termination of 3 months notice on either side. The notice shall be in writing either side. The company may pay the equivalent of three months basic pay and dearness allowances, if any, in lieu of notice or may deduct a like amount when the employee has failed to give due notice".

In the letters of offer of employment to the employees, this rule is expressly brought to their notice stating that it is one of terms and conditions of employment contract. While accepting the employment the candidates have to clearly say that they understood the service rules of the company and that they knew that the rules from part of the service contract, and further that they agree out of their free choice.

The company removed 10 of their employees by invoking the above condition in the service contract (i.e., by passing 3 months notice as per the contract and also by following other procedural legal requirements.). the employees approached the court contending that they cannot be removed.
The lower court held that as per the contract their services can be terminated. The High Court reversed the Judgement of the Lower Court. The matter came up to the Supreme Court.
The question is, is the contract valid? Decide?
A contractor executed several civil works worth Rs.10 crores for a public sector company. The work was delayed. Each party attributed delay to the other party.

The contractor claimed extra payment of Rs.90 lakhs contending that his costs have gone up because of delay on the part of company. Further he disputed the measurements of various items taken by the engineer of the company. According to him if correct measurements are taken he would get Rs.20 lakhs extra. Further he claimed an extra amount of Rs.60 lakhs on the ground that certain works ordered by the engineer were the extra works not mentioned in the contract. He also claimed Rs.10 lakhs towards the extra cost incurred by him on account of deviations in plans ordered by the engineer of the company.

The company on its part refused the claims of the contractor. The company claimed Rs.25 lakhs from the contractor on account of delay. The company claimed that the extra works were not authorised by the engineer and deviations were those of the contractor only. The company contended that measurements were correct.
There was a protracted correspondence between the parties. Several rounds of negotiations were held. Ultimately on 1/8/2000, the contractor has written a letter as follows:
'I want matter to be sorted our amicably without going to court. Notwithstanding my earlier claims, for the sake of amicable settlement, I agree to settle matter on the following basis':
Delay of the work is not due to the fault of anybody.
The measurements taken by your engineer as recorded in the measurement book are correct.
I should be paid Rs.50 lakhs towards the extra works.
No extra cost on account of deviations.
The company received the above letter of the contractor on 5/8/2000 and issued a fax message on 5/8/2000 to the following effect:
'We accept your statements contained in point numbers 1,2 and 4 of your letter dt.1/8/2000. However, we are not prepared to pay Rs.50 lakhs as demanded by you. We shall pay you Rs.10 lakhs only.
The contractor issued a fax message on 6/8/2000: 'I do not accept your proposed payment as a measure of setttlement'.

The company stopped further correspondence. The contractor approached the Arbitrator with a claim of Rs.1 crore and 80 lakhs as originally demanded by him. Arbitrator gave his award for Rs.80 lakhs awarding some amount under each head. The contention of the company that by virtue of the letter dated 1/8/2000 of the contractor and the message dated 5/8/2000 of the company, all other issues cannot be agitated by the contractor except the issue of extra works, was rejected by the Arbitrator. The matter came up to Supreme Court. The company argued that only "extra works" can be subject matter of dispute and the others should be excluded. Decide.

A Government company invited tenders for sale of stocks of damaged food grains. Tenders were opened on 18-5-2000; and the offers were to remain open for acceptance upto 17-7-2000. 'A' was the highest bidder. However, the company was not satisfied  with the highest bid and it invited all the tenderers to participate in the negotiations on 9-6-2000. 'A' refused to revise his bid which was Rs.500/- per quintal. The highest bid during negotiations was Rs.535.72 per quintal. Overall the company was offered an excess amount of Rs.50 lakhs for the entire stock in the highest offers made during negotiations than the amount the company would have received by accepting the original highest bid (Pre negotiations bid). During the negotiations all the tenderers including 'A' were given equal opportunity to participate. ‘A’ participated without prejudice.

'A' filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the refusal of the Government company to accept the highest tender submitted by him claiming that the company, having chosen to invite tenders, could not thereafter dispose of the stocks of damaged food grains by subsequent negotiations rejecting the highest tender on the ground that a higher bid was obtained by negotiations. He was having a legitimate expectation that his bid would be accepted. The action of the company was alleged to be unreasonable, arbitrary and therefore, in substance, violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India. The High Court by its impugned order accepted this contention of 'A' and allowed the writ petition. The company filed SLP in Supreme Court. Whether the procedure followed by the company was legally in order? Decide.
Government of Orissa enacted Orissa Kendu leaves (Control of Trade) Act of 1961 under which the state assumed monopoly of trade in Kendu leaves (they are used in manufacture of bidis).

Under Section 3 of the Act no person other than the Government or its agents or its authorized officers shall purchase or transport Kendu leaves. Under Section 4, the price at which the leaves would be purchased from growers shall be fixed by the Government. Under Section 8, purchasing agents are appointed. Later on Kendu leaves are sold to various parties by the Government. Not less than half of the profits derived by the Government was paid to Panchayat Samitis and Gram Panchayats. Section 10 of the Act provides as follows:
"Kendu leaves purchased by Government or by their officers or agents under this Act shall be sold or otherwise disposed of in such manner as the Government may direct".

In a particular year the State Government in exercise of powers conferred by Section 10 of the Act decided to invite offers for advance purchase of Kendu leaves only from persons who purchased these leaves during the previous year and who acted as purchasers without default to the satisfaction of the Government and the method of sale by open auction, which was adopted during the Government and the method of sale by  open auction, which was adopted during the two previous years, was given up.

One Sri Rashbihari Panda, the petitioner before the Court, who was not the purchaser during the previous two years, now offered a better price than the others but his offer was not considered because the invitation to offer had been restricted to previous years purchasers only.

The petitioner challenged the action of Government in not considering his offer before the High Court of Orissa contending mainly that restricting invitation to offer only to a few classes of persons is illegal and violative of his fundamental rights. The Government contended before the High Court that Section 10 of the Act gives unrestricted power to the Government in the manner of disposal of Kendu leaves and the discretion exercised by Government was not amenable to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court. The Government further demonstrated before the court that the price received during the relevant year is higher than the last two years.

The High Court of Orissa held that the Government's exercises of power of discretion under Section 10 cannot be questioned as the Act has given power to the Government to dispose of the leaves in any manner either by advance purchase contracts or by public auction or by tender. It was held that the court is not concerned with the propriety of Government's action in adopting particular manner of sale. The High Court dismissed the writ petition.
The petitioner filed special leave of appeal in the Supreme Court. Decide?

On behalf of a public sector company its Chief Materials Manager (CMM) has issued an advertisement in various newspapers for sale of some scrap items by auction. The advertisement contains the date of auction and several other details. Some of the conditions relating to the auction mentioned in the advertisement are as follows:
Total material to be auctioned is 1.2 lakhs units and the successful bidders should lift the materials at the rate of 10,000 units per month for twelve months.
Bids should be made on rate basis i.e., rate for 100 units.
For participating in the auction an intending bidder shall make Earnest Money Deposit of Rs.2 lakhs.
The bidder to whom the scrap is sold shall pay 1/6th of the total price for the entire quantity to be lifted during the year within seven days of the date of auction.
E.M.D. of Rs.2 lakhs paid by the bidder shall be adjusted towards the 1/6th amount mentioned in the previous clause and the balance has to be paid by the bidder.
The remaining 5/6th of the amount shall be paid by the bidder in five equal installments (the first installment commencing two months after the date of auction).

CMM will provisionally accept the sale. However the CMM is under no obligation to issue sale letter to any person until he is assured of financial status of the bidder (for which an enquiry can be made by CMM if necessary).

All bids will be made subject to the final confirmation by the Managing Director who is empowered to reject any bid without assigning any reason: and in case the bid of the highest bidder which is accepted by CMM is not confirmed by the Managing Director the entire amount paid by the highest bidder till the date will be refunded without any interest. No bid can be withdrawn after CMM has accepted the bid and the matter is under consideration of the Managing Director and if the bid is withdrawn EMD will be forfeited.

If the successful bidder commits any breach of conditions of sale, the  Earnest Deposited will be forfeited and the material can be sold to any other person either by an auction or by private negotiation and difference in price (shortage) can be recovered from the original successful bidder.
All intending bidders should sign a declaration that they understood the conditions of the auction and that they would abide by the same.
One 'A' made a deposit of Rs.2 lakhs, signed a declaration form agreeing to

.the terms and conditions of the auction. His bid at the rate of Rs.10,000/- per 100 units was accepted by CMM. While matter was pending for confirmation before the Managing Director, 'A' faxed letters to CMM as well as the Managing Director the next day after the auction stating that he withdraws his bid and requesting for return of Rs.2 lakhs E.M.D. paid by him. CMM replied on the third day of auction that under the conditions of the auction, which were agreed by 'A', he cannot withdraw the bid when the matter was pending before Managing Director and hence his request for return of E.M.D. cannot be considered. Further 'A' was informed that he should pay 1/6th of the total amount, i.e., Rs.20 lakhs (at the rate of Rs.10,000/- per 100 units for 1.2 lakh units total amount is Rs.1.2.crores) and he was called upon to pay Rs.18 lakhs net (because E.M.D. of Rs.2 lakhs were adjustabl) within six days of auction.

'A' did not deposit 1/6th of the total amount as called upon by CMM. After expiry of seven days after the date of auction the Managing Director refused confirmation of sale by auction in favour of 'A' on the ground that he did not pay 1/6th of the amount within seven days of auction. His E.M.D. was also forfeited. Further the material was sold in an auction to 'B' for lesser price and a legal notice was served upon 'A' to pay shortage in the price on selling the material to 'B'. 'A' served a legal notice on the company to refund him his E.M.D. with interest.
'A' filed a suit against the company for refund of E.M.D. with interest. The company filed a suit against 'A' for the loss suffered by the company while selling the material for lesser price to 'B'.

The trial court decreed the suit of 'A' and dismissed the suit of the company. In appeal a single judge of the High Court reversed he finding of the trial court and allowed the appeal filed by the company. Division Bench of the High Court restored the findings of the trial court. The company filed a Special Leave Petition before Supreme Court. Decide.

A company (hereinafter referred to as 'purchaser') entered into two separate contracts with a property developer (hereinafter referred to as 'vendor') (1) for purchase of Ac.40.00 cents of land and (2) for construction of a specified number of residential buildings in the land to be purchased. The object of these contracts is to provide a mini township for the employees of the company. The agreement for the purchase of land contains, inter alia, the following stipulations.
The vendor shall convey the land to the purchasers within six months from the date of the agreement and get the registration done.
The total sale consideration shall be Rs.200 lakhs.
On the date of execution of the agreement for sale an amount of Rs.5 lakhs was paid as Earnest money deposit by the purchaser and the said fact is mentioned in the agreement.

Within one month from the date of agreement the vendor shall satisfy the purchaser about the title of the vendor in respect of land in question and if he failed to do so the earnest money paid by the purchaser shall be refunded with interest at the rate of 18% p.a.
Within one month from the date of agreement after satisfying about the title, further amount of Rs.45 lakhs shall be paid.
Within two months after the payment of Rs.45 lakhs mentioned above, further amount of Rs.50 lakhs shall be paid and the purchaser shall be put in possession of the land.

On the date of registration of the land (for which fifteen days notice should be give by the vendor), purchaser should pay the remaining Rs.100 lakhs (on that day the earnest money shall be treated as part of price of land).

If the purchaser fails to pay any installment within the stipulated period, the vendor shall be discharged of his obligation to sell the land and the amounts paid upto the date of breach by the purchaser shall be deemed to be forfeited and the agreement cancelled.

If the vendor fails to give delivery of possession of the land to the purchaser on the due date or if he fails to get the registration done on the due date, the purchaser shall be freed from all the contractual obligations and the vendor shall pay double the amount received by him upto the date of breach by him.
If for any reason the land is not conveyed to the purchaser, the other agreement for construction of residential units shall be deemed to have been cancelled.

Within one month from the date of agreement vendor could satisfy the purchaser about his title to the land and the purchaser paid the first installment of Rs.45 lakhs. Within fifteen days of the payment of the first installment a major accident occurred in the plant of the purchaser company and it suffered loss of about 50 crores on account of the accident. In the changed circumstances, the board of the company decided to postpone the proposal of constructing the township for the employees by another two years and decided to repudiate the contracts with the vendor. Meanwhile the prices of the lands in the area in which the purchasers proposed to purchase the land shot up substantially due to heavy demand for the land. The employees of the company agitated before the management that if the present proposal to purchase the land is shelved it would be impossible to purchase the land in that area after next two years unless the company is prepared to pay double the price. Their contention was that inspite of

the loss caused by the accident the financial position of the company is excellent and hence township should be build as originally planned. In fact the company was in sound financial position notwithstanding the accident.

Inspite of opposition from its employees the company served a notice on the vendor repudiating the agreement for sale of land and demanding the vendor to refund Rs.50 lakhs received by him (which includes earnest money of Rs.5 lakhs) till the date of notice. The said notice was received by the vendor exactly on the last date of expiry of two months from the date of execution of the agreement.

The vendor refused to refund the amount as demanded by the purchaser.  Instead, he served a notice stating that the entire amount Rs.50 lakhs received by him stood forfeited in terms of the agreement.

The purchaser filed a suit against the vendor for recovery of Rs.50 lakhs with interest at 18% p.a. from the date of suit till the date of realisation of the amount. The trial court passed a decree as prayed for holding that the vendor did not suffer any loss on account of cancellation because the land price were shot up meanwhile. In fact the court remarked that the vendor should be thankful to the purchaser for cancellation of agreement because it gives a substantial profit to the vendor. However, the High Court reversed the trial court findings and dismissed the suit holding that forfeiture of the entire amount by the vendor was strictly as per the terms of the agreement the sanctity of which should be maintained. The matter came up before the Supreme Court. Decide.

'A' is the owner of land measuring 200 Acres. B is an estate agent. 'C&CO' is a public sector company (hereinafter referred to as 'the company') which is in need of land for the purpose of construction of quarters for their employees. Though the company has not requested 'B' to negotiate with 'A' for the purchase of land, 'B' approached 'A' and informed 'A' about the intention of purchasing land by the company.
On 1st April, 2000 'A' wrote a letter to the company as follows:

"I hereby agree to sell my land of 200 acres (particulars given) in favour of your company subject to your paying me Rs.50 lakhs at your option on or before 30-6-2000 by cash or bank draft. During the next three months I swear, I shalal not enter into deal with any body and you have full three months time to take benefit of this agreement at your choice".
On 30th May, 2000 one 'P' a private firm offered to purchase the land of 'A'  at the cost of Rs.75 lakhs.
On the afternoon of 30th May, 2000 'A' issued a fax message to the company (followed by confirmation by post) to the following effect.
'Please refer to my letter dt.1-4-2000. As I received a better offer I do not want to sell my land to your company and kindly treat my letter as withdrawn'.
Fax message sent by 'A' was seen by the authorised officer of the company on 30th May, 2000 itself. Confirmation copy was received on 5th June, 2000. On
6th June, 2000 the company issued a fax message to 'A' as follows:

"We do not agree for the withdrawal of your earlier agreement contained in your letter dt.1-4-2000. We shall send the amount of Rs.50 lakhs on or before  was to 30-6-2000". 'A' did not give any reply.

On 20th June, 2000 the company issued another letter to 'A' (which was received by 'A' on 28th June) requesting 'A' to execute the sale deed for land of 200 acres. A bank draft for Rs.50 lakhs was enclosed to the letter.

'A' returned the Bank draft to the company and entered into an agreement for sale with 'P' for consideration of Rs.75 lakhs. As per the agreement the sale deed would be executed in favour of the 'P' on 15th July, 2000.

The company filed a suit on 10th July, 2000 showing 'A' and 'P' as defendants with the following prayers (1) for directing 'A' to sell the land to the company as agreed by 'A' in his letter dt.1-4-2000 and (2) for permanent injunction restraining 'A' from selling the land in question to 'P' or to any other person except 'A'.

The trial court decided the matter in favour of the company and granted reliefs as prayed for. The High Court reversed the judgement and directions of the trial court. The company approached the Supreme Court will it succeed? Decide.

'M' a contractor entered into a contract with a public sector company for supply of electrical goods for one year and deposited Rs.75,000/- for the due performance of contract. The contract contained a risk purchase clause and also a  provision to  forfeit deposit in case of breach of contract. After some initial supplies, there was some lapse on the part of 'M' and the company, in pursuance of the terms of the contract rescinded the contract and forfeited the amount deposited by the plaintiff.

'M' filed suit for recovery of Rs.75,000/- from the company. The company has not adduced any evidence to show that the company suffered some loss on account of breach of contract by 'M' but argued in the court that in view of a clear clause in the contract that the deposit amount would be forfeited in case of breach of contract by 'M', it is justified in forfeiture. The company further argued that the deposit amount was Earnest Money Deposit and it could be forfeited. 'M' argued it cannot be forfeited unless some loss is shown to have been caused on account of breach by him.

The trial court dismissed the suit. A single judge of High Court reversed the order of the lower court and held that 'M' is entitled to recover the amount. A division bench of the High Court reversed the finding of the single judge and upheld the judgement of the trial court. 'M' filed SLP in Supreme Court. The contentions of the parties in the trial court were repeated in the Supreme Court. Will 'M' succeed or whether forfeiture by the company will be upheld. Decide.

'S' is a contractor who entered into a contract for purchase of some metal scrap items from a public sector company for Rs.200 lakhs of Rupees. As per the terms of contract 'S' was to pay Rs.20 lakhs, being 10% of the contract price, on the date of the agreement. The remaining price was to be paid in 10 equal monthly installments. The initial deposit will be adjusted in the final bills. A schedule for lifting of the stock was also given. The contract contained a clause to the effect that if the contractor failed to pay balance purchase price, the company is entitled to cancel the contract and forfeit the amount deposited at the time of contract. There is a risk purchase clause also.

The contractor failed to pay the balance price and the company forfeited the deposit. The contractor filed a suit for recovery of the amount forfeited. In the trial court no evidence was adduced on behalf of the company that any loss was suffered by it on account of default by it. The trial court held that deposit cannot be forfeited. A single judge of the High Court held that amount can be forfeited. A division bench held that amount cannot be forfeited. The matter came up to Supreme Court.
Whether the company is justified in forfeiture of whether 'S' can recover the amount. Decide.
C A S E S T U D Y No: 12

The Public Sector Corporation issued a notice inviting tenders for purchase of some of the articles to be sold by that Corporation. The terms and conditions of the tender are mentioned in the notice. The last date of submission of tenders was 23-3-2000. The tenders were to be submitted before 4.00 p.m. on that date. At 5.00 p.m. the tenders would be opened. Five parties tendered their documents and papers. However, in view of an interim order of the High Court, the Corporation could not open tenders till 24-3-2000. One of the parties “M & Co.” failed to attach demand draft for requisite amount towards earnest money deposit even though the said party had got deposited the amount in one of the nationalised banks by 3.00 p.m. on 23-3-2000. The said bank was 200 k.m. away from the place of the Corporation where tenders were to be opened. A fax copy of the demand draft was attached to the tender documents. On the morning of 24-3-2000, five hours before opening of the tenders, the Managing Director of that Corporation took a decision that earnest money need not be deposited by a tenderer if the tenderer was a small scale industry. “M & Co.” was small scale industry. On 24-3-2000 the tenders were opened and the tender of ‘M’ was accepted being the highest amount offered. The offer of one ‘K’ was the next highest.

‘K’ challenged the award of contract to ‘M’ mainly on the ground that ‘M’ did not submit original demand draft towards earnest money before 4.00 p.m. on 23-3-2000. ‘K’ prayed the court to direct the Corporation to award contract to him by setting aside the award of contract to ‘M’. The matter came up to Supreme Court. Decide?
C A S E S T U D Y No: 13

A Public Sector Organisation issued a tender notice inviting tenders for supply of some articles which are used in the final products manufactured by that Organisation. 13 companies which are manufacturers of all that particular material submitted tenders in response to the tender notification. Out of those 13 companies, 10 companies are in the small scale industries and the remaining are bigger manufacturers. All of them submitted tenders quoting the rate for 100 units of the material required by the Public Sector Organisation in terms of the tender notification. The price quoted for 100 units by the 3 bigger manufacturers is exactly same i.e., Rs.77,666/-, the remaining tenderers quoted higher price ranging from Rs.83,000/- to Rs.85,000/- per month.

A tender committee of the Public Sector Organisation scrutinized all the tenders and formed an opinion that the 3 big manufacturers formed a cartel and deliberately quoted a lower price just to eliminate the competition from the other manufacturers. According to the tender Committee workable price would be Rs.79,305/- for 100 units which was incidentally the contract price during the previous year. After the last date of receiving the tenders was over, the Government of India granted some tax concessions which had the effect of reducing the cost of the material for which tenders were called by the Public Sector Organisation. So, after announcing of such concessions, two of the three bigger manufacturers sent a revised offer of Rs.67,000/- per 100 units.

The entire matter was considered by the Director (Finance) of the Public Sector Organisation and it was decided to place order on all the manufacturers who submitted tenders because the requirement was for a huge quantity of the material. He thought that if the orders were placed only on the bigger manufacturers, the smaller manufacturers would have to close down their units because they were like ancillary industries whose products are useful only to the public sector organisation. It was observed by the Director (Finance) that if orders are placed only on the bigger manufacturers, it would drive out smaller manufacturers from the field and in the future period only bigger manufacturers will remain in the field and they will have opportunity to raise price according to their will. So he felt in the long term interest of the Company, orders should be placed on all the manufacturers. He proposed that a counter offer should be given by the Public Sector Organisation to all the 13 companies who originally submitted the tenders with a dual price system. It was decided that Rs.76,000/- per 100 units is the reasonable price after the concessions are announced by the Government and accordingly the counter offers should be made fixing Rs.76,000/- as the price for all the smaller manufacturers. However, for bigger manufacturers, an offer was made fixing Rs.67,000/- because that was revised price offered by those two manufacturers.

Ultimately all the 13 manufacturers were issued counter offers by the Public Sector Organisation offering higher price to the smaller manufacturers and lower price to the two bigger manufacturers. The two bigger manufacturers filed a writ petition in the High court contending that such discriminatory offer is in violation of Article 14 of the Constitution of India and that they also should be offered the same price which was offered to the remaining 11 manufacturers. The High Court allowed the writ petition specifically observing that the sole aim of the Public Sector Organisation should be to maximise its profits, which would mean profit to the public, which can be ensured by accepting the best offers of the two bigger manufacturers to the exclusion of the remaining manufacturers. Alternatively, the Court held that all the manufacturers should be offered the same price that was initially quoted by the bigger manufacturers i.e., the offer should have been Rs.67,000/- per 100 units for all the manufacturers.

Aggrieved by the decision of the High Court, the Public Sector Organisation filed SLP in the Supreme Court. It was contended before the Supreme Court that in the circumstance of the case dual pricing system was lawfully valid. The two bigger manufacturers contended that the High Court was right in striking down the dual pricing system of the public sector organisation because such system was discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India.
If you are one of the judges of the Supreme Court how do you decide the case?
C A S E S T U D Y No: 14

Cochin International Airport Limited (for brevity sake referred to as ‘CIAL’) is a Public Sector undertaking. It has been established for setting up and maintaining a new International Airport at Cochin. For awarding a contract for ground-handling facilities at the new Airport it invited offers by writing letters to some companies having experience of that type. The letters were written on       12-11-97 to Cambatta Aviation Ltd., (hereinafter referred to has ‘Cambatta’), Air India and six others. The last date for receipt of proposals were 31-12-97. Cambatta, Air India and three other companies (those three are foreign companies) responded. On 13-7-98 ‘CIAL’ again wrote to them to make their best offers on or before 28-7-98. Only Air India and Cambatta made fresh proposals.

The committee constituted by ‘CIAL’ for evaluation of the offers met on 28-9-98. Except one foreign company, the remaining were on a par as regards technical competence, organisational capacity and past experience. The committee took note of the fact that ‘Cambatta’ and ‘Air India’ are Indian organisations, operate mainly in India and have better proven adaptability for operating in Indian conditions. Out of those two it recommended Cambatta for awarding the work on the ground that Cambatta’s financial rating was found higher. However, the committee had in its minutes noted that financial rating cannot be the sole criterion for taking the final decision. On 11-8-98 the Government of India wrote a letter to the Government of Kerala recommending Air India for awarding the contract on the ground that Air India is the national carrier and has better experience. Thereafter a meeting took place between the Managing Director of Air India and the Chief Minister of Kerala. This was followed by a letter dated 29-10-98 by the Managing Director of Air India to the Chief Minister of Kerala seeking an opportunity to make a more detailed presentation to the Board of CIAL on the advantages CIAL would derive if Air India was appointed its exclusive handling agent. The Board of Directors met on 7-11-98 and decided to have a detailed discussion with Air India before taking a final decision and informed it to give a presentation before the Board on 27-11-98. After the presentation, Air India slightly revised their offer regarding the license fee to be paid to CIAL so that it would match the offer of Cambatta. Finally the contract was awarded to Air India on 12-12-98. Meanwhile, between 10-11-98 to 7-12-98 Cambatta wrote four letters to CIAL protesting against giving preference to a national carrier in view of the policy of liberalisation, giving further opportunity for Air India to make a presentation to the Board, going back upon its earlier decision to give contract to Cambatta and allowing Air India to revise its offer behind the back of Cambatta. Cambatta contended that the action of CIAL would be unfair, unethical and violative of the limited Global competitive building norms. CIAL has not given reply to any of these letters.

Cambatta filed a writ petition in the Kerala High Court challenging the action of CIAL in awarding contract to Air India especially when the offer of Cambatta was the highest and it had fulfilled all the conditions. The further contention was that CIAL had not acted fairly and impartially as it had carried on negotiations with Air India behind the back of Cambatta and no opportunity was given to Cambatta to give a better offer. In the counter affidavit filed on behalf of CIAL it was stated that this was not a case where tenders were invited. It was a project to be implemented by raising finances from various sources and, therefore, it was decided to invite offers from reputed agencies in order to decide best terms and conditions and then to award the contract to the best suited party in order to make the project viable and successful. It was further stated that individual offers were assessed considering the background and infrastructure of the companies, their financial capacity, expertise and future benefits likely to accrue to CIAL. While awarding the contract to Air India what had weighed with it was, apart from its selection by the evaluating Committee, that it is a public sector unit, the national carrier under the Government of India and that it had offered to support CIAL in a big way by showing its willingness in equity participation. It had also taken into consideration the fact that Cambatta was not an airline operator like Air India and its interest and expertise was limited to ground-handling work alone. Air India had also offered to help in improving the revenue of CIAL by increasing air traffic through the Cochin Airport. Thus, on a comparative analysis of the offers made by Cambatta and Air India it was found that the offer made by Air India was better and more beneficial to CIAL.

The petition was heard by a learned Single Judge of the High Court who held that there was no illegality, arbitrariness or unreasonableness in the decision-making process of CIAL and the decision was taken bona fide after evaluating both the offers and on being satisfied that in the matter of experience, expertise, infrastructure and financial capacity the offer of Air India was superior and more beneficial. As regards the allegation of actual mala fides the learned Single Judge held that the pleading in that behalf was very vague and scanty.

The matter was then carried by Cambatta in appeal before the same High Court. The Division Bench held that it was a case of public tender. It also held that though the decision of the Evaluation Committee was only recommendatory and not binding on the Board of Directors of CIAL, the fact that the Evaluation Committee had considered all the relevant aspects and found Cambatta as the most competent party and yet no reasons were disclosed for explaining what prompted the Board of Directors to take a different view was clearly indicative of the fact that CIAL was influenced in its decision-making process by Air India and the Secretary of the Ministry of Civil Aviation. It was also of the view that if the other tenderers had also been invited for negotiations by CIAL then possibly they would have given better offers and pointed out the demerits of the offers made by the rival tenderers. It held that the Board of Directors was influenced by the threat to the effect that if Air India was not given the contract, the international airport would be bereft of flights as Air India would not allow other flights to land there. It then held that the action of CIAL in awarding contract to Air India was arbitrary, illegal and opposed to the principles of natural justice. It allowed the appeal, cancelled the contract in favour of Air India and directed CIAL to reconsider the valid tenders once again and, if necessary, to call all those tenderers for negotiations before finalising the contract.

The Supreme Court considered the scope of Article 14 vis-à-vis contracts with public body and held that public bodies who come under 'state' have to conform to Article 14 of the constitution of which non arbitrariness is a significant fact. A public authority possesses powers only to use them for public good. This imposes a duty to act fairly and to adopt a procedure which is 'fair play in action'. Due observance of this obligation as a part of good administration raises a reasonable or legitimate expectation in every citizen to be treated fairly in his interaction with the state. To satisfy this requirement of non arbitrariness in state action, it is, therefore necessary to consider and give due weight to the reasonable or legitimate expectations of the persons likely to be affected by the decision or else that unfairness in the exercise of the power may amount to an abuse or excess of power apart from affecting the bonafides of the decision in a given case. The decision so made would be exposed to challenge on the ground of arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the excise of power, as it is unrealistic, but provides for control of its exercise by judicial review.

A procedure wherein resort is had to negotiations with the tenderers for obtaining significantly higher bid during the period when the offers in the tenders remain open for acceptance and rejection of the tenders only in the event of a significant higher bid being obtained during negotiations would ordinarily satisfy this requirement. This procedure involves giving due weight to the legitimate expectation of the highest bidder to have his tender accepted unless outbid by a highest offer, in which case acceptance of the highest offer within the time the offers remain open would be a reasonable exercise of power for public good.

"…………. Section 74 declares the law as to liability upon breach of contract where  compensation is by agreement of parties predetermined (liquidated damages) or where there is a stipulation by a way of penalty ………. The court has to adjudge in every case reasonable compensation to which the plaintiff is entitled from the defendant on the breach of contract. Such compensation has to be ascertained having regard to the conditions existing on the date of breach".

"………..The section undoubtedly says that the aggrieved party is entitled to receive compensation from the party who has broken the contract, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused by the breach. Thereby it merely dispenses with proof of 'actual loss or damage'; it does not justify the award of compensation when in consequence of the breach no legal injury at all has resulted, because compensation for breach of contract can be awarded to make good loss or damage which naturally arose in the usual course of things or which the parties knew when they made the contract, to be likely result from breach".

In para 7 of the judgement, the Supreme Court noted the law on the subject which is as follows:

“7. The law relating to award of a contract by the State, its corporations and bodies acting as instrumentalities and agencies of the Government has been settled by the decisions of this Court in the following cases:
Ramana Dayaram Shetty Vs International Airport Authority of India – (1979) 3 SCC 489.
Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union (Regd.) Vs Union of India – (1981) 1 SCC 568.
CCE Vs Dunlop India Limited – (1985) 1 SCC 260:1985 SCC (Tax) 75.
Tata Cellular Vs Union of India – (1994) 6 SCC 651.
Ramniklal N. Bhutta Vs State of Maharastra – (1997) 1 SCC 134.
Raunaq International Ltd., Vs I.V.R. Construction Ltd., (1999) 1 SCC 492.

The award of a contract, whether it is by a private party or by a public body or the State, is essentially a commercial transaction. In arriving at a commercial decision considerations which are paramount are commercial considerations. The State can choose its own method to arrive at a decision. It can fix its own terms of invitation to tender and that is not open to judicial scrutiny. It can enter into negotiations before finally deciding to accept one of the offers made to it. Price need not always be the sole criterion for awarding a contract. It is free to grant any relaxation, for bona fide reasons, if the tender conditions permit such a relaxation. It may not accept the offer even though it happens to be the highest or the lowest. But the State, its corporations, instrumentalities and agencies are bound to adhere to the norms, standards and procedures laid down by them and cannot depart from them arbitrarily. Though that decision is not amenable to judicial review, the court can examine the decision-making process and interfere if it is found vitiated by mala fides, unreasonableness and arbitrariness. The State, its corporations, instrumentalities and agencies have the public duty to be fair to all concerned. Even when some defect is found in the decision-making process the court must exercise its discretionary power under Article 226 with great caution and should exercise it only in furtherance of public interest and not merely on the making out of a legal point. The court should always keep the larger public interest in mind in order to decide whether its intervention is called for or not. Only when it comes to a conclusion that overwhelming public interest requires interference, the court should intervene.

The Supreme Court considered the rival contentions keeping in view of the facts of the case. Regarding the contention of Cambatta that CIAL should not have negotiated with Air India behind the back of Cambatta and should not have permitted Air India to revised its offer, the Supreme Court noted that even though  Cambatta wrote several protest letters it had not requested CIAL to give it any opportunity to negotiate or to improve upon its offer. The court further noted that the decision of the committee was not final and it was not binding on the Board of Directors. The Board of Directors, at the meeting held on 7-11-98, considered the proposals of Air India and Cambatta and appeared to have taken a tentative decision to award the contract to Air India and, therefore called it for negotiations with a view to have better terms and take a final decision. The final decision was taken on 27-11-98 as Air India agreed to make its offer more beneficial to CIAL. The Board of Directors having taken a tentative decision on 7-11-98 there was no point in calling Cambatta thereafter for any negotiation. The Supreme Court noted that Cambatta was recommended over Air India by the committee only because Cambatta’s financial rating was found higher, which, even according to the committee cannot be sole criterion for taking the final decision. More over, in a commercial transaction of such a complex nature a lot of balancing work has to be done while weighing all the relevant factors and the final decision has to be taken after taking overall view of the transaction.

The Supreme Court specifically observed that CIAL did not do any wrong in taking into consideration the fact that Air India is an Indian airline and being a national carrier would be in a position to bring more traffic of Air India and other domestic airlines if it was awarded the contract. Regarding the argument of Cambatta that its offer was better than that of Air India, the court held that it would not be proper to look at only the financial aspect. In a commercial transaction of a complex nature what may appear to be better, on the face of it, may not be considered so when an overall view is taken. In such matters the court cannot substitute its decision for the decision of the party awarding the contract. On the basis of the material placed on record, the court found that CIAL bona fide believed that involving a public sector undertaking and a national carrier would, in the long run, prove to be more beneficial to CIAL.

Ultimately the Supreme Court held that the decision of the High Court holding that CIAL had acted arbitrarily and unreasonably and was also influenced by extraneous considerations during its decision-making process is wrong and set aside the judgement of the Division Bench of the High Court.

CHAIRMAN’S ADDRESS
                                      Dear Shareholders
                                      I take great pleasure in welcoming you all for the 33rd Annual General
                                      Meeting of your Company. I take this opportunity to thank you all
                                      for making it convenient to attend the meeting and express my
                                      gratitude for your continuous support and patronage for improved
                                      performance. The Directors’ Report, the Audited Statement of
                                      Accounts for the year 2014-15 and the Notice to the Shareholders
                                      have already been circulated and with your permission, I take them
                                      as read.
                                      External Environment
                                    Challenges are being faced by the steel industry world wide with
                                    slowdown in global economies. The outlook for global steel demand
    suggests a low growth period ahead, as per World Steel Association. There was a growth of 0.7% in
    steel demand globally during 2014, which is projected to decrease by 1.7% in 2015.
    During 2014-15, the Indian economy growth picked up, helped by positive policies and lower crude
    oil prices. As per ADB projections, growth in GDP is expected to accelerate to 7.4% in 2015 on
    improved performance by both industry and services. Growth is expected to edge up further to 7.8%
    in 2016, helped by a supportive monetary policy in 2015, as inflation continues to trend lower and
    pick-up in capital expenditure.
    Your Company’s performance
    During the 1st half of the year, the Company achieved 9% growth in Crude Steel production. However,
    the operations of the company were severely impacted by Cyclone ‘Hudhud’ on 12th October, 2014.
    After the Cyclone, all out efforts were made by the Company for early recovery and to make up for the
    shortfall in production during the balance months.
    In the 2nd half, the company also had to bear the brunt of cheap imports from China – which is facing
    demand recession – and Russia and Ukraine, where major currency devaluation remains export-
    supportive. There was a considerable pressure on margins due to unfavourable market conditions
    characterized by significant increase in cheaper imports pulling the prices down significantly. As a
    result, the company could achieve Profit after Tax of 62.30 Cr only during the year.
    However, the company has commissioned all major units of expansion to 6.3 mtpa of liquid steel.
    The company is also modernizing some of its existing assets, which will further increase the capacity
    to 7.3 mtpa and help in maintaining its techno economic supremacy. These initiatives along with
    other strategic initiatives being pursued would place the company in good stead in the coming years.
    Sustainability initiatives
    The Corporate Plan of the Company was revised during the year envisaging a growth target of
    16 Mtpa by 2025. The Vision statement has been articulated “To be the most efficient steel maker
    having the largest single location shore based steel plant in the country”.
    Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)
    CSR activities continue to play a pivotal role with focus on inclusive sustainable growth. In the year
    2014-15, the emphasis was on society care and provision of welfare measures to the needy. A
    separate section is provided in Directors’ Report regarding CSR activities.


4                                                                                                              4

Corporate Governance
Your company’s commitment to transparency in Corporate Governance is reflected in its establishing
appropriate systems and procedures for every process. A separate Report on Corporate Governance
alongwith Certificate on Compliances of CG guidelines and Secretarial Audit / Compliance forms part
of the Directors’ Report.
Environment Management
As a manufacturing company, RINL is conscious of its role in maintaining clean environment for
future generation. Your Company has been conducting Mass Plantation Melas to bring awareness
and create responsibility. A separate section on the same forms part of the Directors’ Report.
Dividend for the year 2014-15
Your Company has declared dividend for the seventh consecutive financial year. For the financial
year 2014-15, the Company paid an Interim Dividend of 14 crores and 11.35 crores on Preference
Shares and Ordinary Equity Shares respectively to Govt of India (GOI). The total dividend pay-out for
the year is 40.64% (previous FY 25.28%) and including dividend tax, it is 48.77% (Previous FY
29.58%) of PAT.
Contribution to the Exchequer
Over the last 30 years, the cumulative accrual to the Government Exchequer in the form of revenue
comprising of excise duty, customs duty, income tax, Sales Tax, entry tax, octroi and other State
levies is around 30642 Crs. I am sure with the increase in production capacity and turnover, the
contribution to Govt exchequer would improve further.
Looking ahead
India is increasingly becoming an important part of the international steel market and a key growth
area for steel production, based on various positive factors including its strong demand for steel
arising from strong economic growth, low per capita steel consumption and abundant iron ore reserves.
The Expansion to 6.3 mtpa will strengthen the position of the company as a market leader in Bars and
Structurals. RINL products will continue to be sought after especially when the long product
consumption in the country is poised for accelerated growth with large scale infrastructural investment
planned by the Government. To tap the potential of export to the neighbouring countries, RINL has
already opened its International Marketing Centre in Colombo, Sri Lanka. The Company is also
actively pursuing partnership through the routes of Joint Venture and Steel Processing Units for the
end users in order to ensure ready/tailor made markets.
Acknowledgement
I acknowledge, on behalf of the Board of Directors that the achievements in the year have been made
possible only due to the relentless and dedicated efforts of RINL collective. I thank all the Stakeholders,
particularly the Ministry of Steel and other Ministries of GoI, the Government of AP, the Suppliers
(Domestic and Overseas), Customers, Ancillary Units, Bankers, the People’s Representatives, the
District Administration and various other agencies for the confidence and trust bestowed upon the
Company and the opportunity given for its continued growth for achieving various milestones.
Thanking you,
Jai Hind,

3.   R&D
     Research & Development in the areas of process improvement, environment protection, waste
     management, cost reduction, new product development and new technology development.
     (a) Improvement of MgO – C brick quality to enhance the converter life
         MgO-C bricks are used for refractory lining of LD Converters. This R&D project was taken
         up jointly with CGCRI, Kolkata. Application of the product developed with the suggested
         formulation has led to enhanced converter life.
     (b) Mathematical modelling of sintering cum pelletisation process
         Mathematical modeling of agglomeration processes like sintering and pelletisation would
         help in process optimization, consistent sinter quality and improvement in productivity in
         sinter plant. The project was taken up in collaboration with IISc, Bangalore.
     (c) Optimization of design and operating parameters like wire speed, bath super heat, steel
         grades on Calcium recovery and its efficacy for inclusion modification
         Alumina is formed during Aluminium deoxidation of steel creating clogging problems during
         casting. A joint research project was taken up with IIT, Kharagpur to mitigate the problem
         by addition of calcium in the liquid steel in the form of Ca-Si and Ca-Fe.
     (d) Effect of iron ore micro-fines on sintering process
         Increased levels of production of steel led to more mining resulting in increase in generation
         of micro fines. These micro fines are left unutilized although they have high iron content.
         Attempts are being made to maximize use of iron ore micro-fines in sintering process. A
         collaborative project was taken up with IMMT, Bhubaneswar for studying the effect of
         micro-fines on sintering process.
     (e) Feasibility studies of enrichment of BF gas for enhancement of calorific value
         Blast furnace (BF) gas has 18-20% of CO gas and its calorific value is 700-850kcal/m3.
         Studies are underway to increase the calorific value by reducing the contents of CO2 and
         N2 in gas mixture. CGCRI, Kolkata is the research partner.
     (f) Development of seismic resistant rebars having improved corrosion resistance
         Thermo Mechanical Treated bars are used in RCC in construction. This internal project
         aims to increase its seismic and corrosion resistance.
     (g) Studies and development of Carbon dioxide (CO2) sequestration technique using LD
         Converter slag (steel slag) to control the Green House Effect of Carbon dioxide
         CO2 emissions and generation of LD slag are some of the major causes of concern for
         steel industry. Sequestration of CO2 making use of the calcium component of LD slag is
         under study. NIOT, Chennai is the collaborative Research Partner.

A. SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
     1.0 GENERAL
        1.1 Financial Statements are prepared under the historical cost convention in accordance with
            fundamental accounting assumptions and Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) in
            India and the relevant provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 including Accounting Standards notified
            there under.
        1.2 The preparation of financial statements in conformity with Generally Accepted Accounting prinicples
            require estimates and assumptions to be made that affect the reported amounts of assets and
            liabilities and disclosure of contingent liabilities on the date of financial statements and the reported
            amounts of revenues and expenses during the reporting Period. Actual results could differ from
            these estimates and differences between actual results and estimates are recognised in the periods
            in which the results are known/materialised.
     2.0 FIXED ASSETS
        2.1 Fixed assets are stated at historical cost less accumfulated depreciation/amortisation.
        2.2 Expenditure attributable / relating to construction is accounted as below :
             (a) To the extent directly identifiable to any specific Plant Unit, Trial run expenditure net of revenue
                 is included in the cost of Fixed asset.
             (b) To the extent not directly indentifiable to any specific Plant Unit, is kept under ‘Expenditure
                 During Construction’ for allocation to Fixed Assets and is grouped under ‘Capital Work-in-
                 Progress’.
     3.0 INVESTMENTS
        3.1 Current investments are carried at lower of cost and fair value.
        3.2 Long-term investments are carried at cost. Diminution in value, other than temporary, is provided
            for.
     4.0 INVENTORIES
        4.1 Inventories are valued at lower of cost and net realizable value.
        4.2 The basis of determining cost is:
        4.2.1Finished / Semi-finished goods, Raw materials - Periodic Weighted Average cost.
        4.2.2Minor Raw materials, Stores & Spares, Loose Tools - Dynamic Moving Weighted Average cost.
        4.2.3All Materials in-transit at cost.
        4.3 Obsolete/ Surplus/ Non-moving inventory are adequately provided for:
     5.0 REVENUE RECOGNITION
        5.1 Sales are recognized when all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred to
            the buyer.
        5.2 Export incentives under various schemes are recognized as Income on certainty of realisation.




98

6.0 CLAIMS
   6.1 Claims against outside agencies are accounted on certainty of realisation.
7.0 FOREIGN CURRENCY TRANSACTIONS
   7.1 Foreign currency monetary items are recorded at the closing rate.
   7.2 Exchange differences arising on account of settlement / conversion of foreign currency monetary
       items are recognised as expense or income in the Period in which they arise.
8.0 EMPLOYEE BENEFITS
   8.1 Provisions/Liabilities towards gratuity, postretirement medical benefits, retirement settlement benefits,
       and Employees’ Family Benefit Scheme are made based on the actuarial valuation as at the end of
       the year. Consequential charge to statement of Profit and Loss includes actuarial gains/losses.
9.0 DEPRECIATION AND AMORTISATION
   9.1 Depreciation is provided on straight line method (SLM), up to 95% of the cost of the asset over their
       useful lives as in Schedule-II of the Companies Act, 2013. except in respect of the following categories
       of assets where their useful life is based on the technical assessment of the Management (useful

Subsidiaries and Joint Ventures
      During the year, the Board of Directors (the Board) reviewed the affairs of subsidiaries and Joint
      Ventures. In accordance with Section 129(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 Consolidated Financial
      Statements had been prepared which form part of the Annual Report. Further, the report on the
      performance and financial position of each of the subsidiary, associate and joint venture and
      salient features of the financial statements in the prescribed Form AOC-1 is annexed to this
      report.
      Subsidiaries:
      1.   Eastern Investment Limited: (EIL)
           The income of the company is derived mainly from (i) dividends from investments in shares
           of various companies including subsidiary company OMDC (ii) interest on term deposits
           with banks and deposits in bonds. The dividend income received from the Orissa Minerals
           Development Company Ltd (OMDC) during the year was 0.31 Crores i.e. 1.04 per each
           share of 1 each compared to 0.97 Crores i.e. 3.22 per share of 1 each in 2013-14.
           The total income of the company for the year ended 31.03.2015 is 1.22 Crores, with loss
           of 12.63 Crores before tax and loss 12.72 Crores after tax.
      2.   Orissa Minerals Development Company Limited : (OMDC)
           There was no mining activity in the mines of OMDC (Company) owing to non-renewal of
           mining leases. The management of the compnay has been putting constant efforts and
           regularly meeting State Governments Officials. The legal issues are also being addressed
           with utmost care by engaging experienced and senior advocates/legal professionals.
           As mines remained inoperative, the company could not earn revenue from operations during
           the year. The company has earned an interest income of 74.02 Crores during the year on
           term deposits, which is included in other income. The company earned profit before tax of
             25.84 Crores as compared to 16.74 Crores in the previous year. Profit after tax stood at
             17.70 Crores as compared to 6.26 Crores during the previous year.
      3.   Bisra Stone Lime Company Limited : (BSLC)
           The performance of the Company during the year was severely affected due to closure of
           mines w.e.f.13.08.2014 in accordance with the order issued by DDM; Rourkela based on
           notification dated 18.07.2014 of Ministry of Mines.
           Based on an appeal preferred by BSLC, the Hon’ble High Court of Odisha allowed resumption
           of mining operations on 02.03.2015. After completion of statutory formalities production
           started from 26.03.2015.
           Sales turnover of the Company has decreased to 7.11 Crores for the current year ended
           on 31st March 2015 from 28.53 Crores during the previous year. Consequently, the operation
           has resulted in loss of 27.27 Crores for the year and the accumulated loss as on 31.03.2015
           stood at 158.14 Crores.




122

Joint Ventures
1.   International Coal Ventures Pvt. Ltd. : (ICVL)
     In a landmark acquisition of large coal mine and coal assets overseas by Indian companies,
     International Coal Ventures Pvt. Ltd. (ICVL), the joint venture of SAIL, Coal India Limited,
     Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited, NMDC Limited & NTPC Limited took over an operating coal
     mine and coal assets of Rio Tinto Limited in Moatize Coal basin in Tete province of
     Mozambique, with a total coal resource of 2.6 billion tonnes. This acquisition has been
     intended to give long term security for supply of a critical raw material for its Promoter
     Companies. The operating coal mine at Benga produces prime hard coking coal / thermal
     coal, and has a state-of-the-art wash plant and surface infrastructure with a potential to
     expand the raw coal production from the current 5 million tonnes per annum (Mtpa) to 12
     Mtpa.
2.   RINMOIL:
     RINL has Joint venture with MOIL for setting up Ferro Alloys Plant. As per TEFR prepared
     by MECON Ltd, the projects are not viable at the present power tariffs of State Electricity
     Boards. Hence, other options to source power at cheaper rates are being explored. In view
     of this, there is no activity in the joint venture company during the year.
