1. Executive Summary
Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd (RINL), a wholly owned company by the Government of India, wanted to revisit its
Corporate Plan 2020 made in the year 2007 and formulate Vision 2027 - Corporate Plan document (revised to
Vision 2025 - Corporate Plan document) in view of the major shifts in external scenario and the company’s
expansion plans. PwC was selected through a competitive bidding process for developing the “Corporate Plan-
Vision 2027” document (revised to Vision 2025 - Corporate Plan document) for RINL. In this context PwC have
submitted an Inception Report on 20th September, 2013 with the approach to be adopted for the assignment,
and an Interim Report on 26th February, 2014 with detailed analysis of the external business environment and
the internal organizational aspects of RINL. PwC submitted a Draft Final Report on 31st March, 2014 with
various strategic options that RINL may adopt. PwC submitted the final report based on the feedback received
on the draft final report on 27th May 2014 which was subsequently approved in December 2014 as “Corporate
Plan- Vision 2025” document so as to match an important growth milestones with the terminal year of vision
2025 of Ministry of Steel. However the planning horizon covered by PwC remains till 2027.
This report starts with a discussion on the key trends in the external business environment. The global steel
industry is cyclic in nature and has seen highs and lows with changing economic scenario. In recent times, the
global economy has faced two significant setbacks – economic crisis of 2009 and the slowdown of 2012. During
both the times, the steel industry was adversely affected as demand for steel contracted sharply, prices
nosedived, trade declined sharply, and production and job cuts were enforced. However, strategies like cost
cutting, focusing on profitable segments & value added products, long term customer contracts, geographical
diversification and achieving economics of scale were some of the strategies adopted by global steel makers to
survive such downturns.
According to the estimates of World Steel Association and PwC analysis, the global steel consumption is
expected to reach 2168 MT by 2027 the major drivers being demand from Asia (including high Indian demand)
and Africa. Indian steel consumption is expected to reach 225 MT by 2027 of which maximum increase in
demand for steel is expected to be in the infrastructure sector which majorly consumes long products. Having
established quality assets, RINL’s Indian peers are now well poised to take advantage of the growth
opportunities and have adopted various strategies like brownfield & green field expansion, entering new
markets & products, backward integration for raw material security, alliances/ JVs with global peers, etc. Thus,
it may be concluded that enhancing business capabilities to suit market conditions will be critical for the long-
term success of steel companies. But, before embarking on a strategic transformation initiative, they need to
determine their current capabilities & where they want to go in order to best plan & leverage the
transformation.
The report also contains an analysis of the current business profile of RINL through the lens of the value chain
analysis framework. Some of the key observations from our analysis are:

        Ensuring Raw Material Security has emerged as one of the most essential objective of RINL.

        RINL, so far has fared well on the technical aspects, however there is a need for continuous operational
         improvement, innovation and adoption of new technologies.

        In the immediate timeframe the challenge is to achieve the rated capacity & maximize the share of value
         added steel. Going forward, Growth through expansion, product & market diversification should be the
         focus of RINL.

        The focus of the Human Resource function in RINL needs to gradually shift from personnel
         management to strategic HR and play key role in building a high performance culture, while at the
         same time strengthening IR at the base.

        RINL performance and cash flows have been under stress in the last few years. Its cash reserves have
         declined due to the expansion activities and RINL is now relying on debt. Funding sources for the next
         phase of expansion is critical for RINL growth.

Based on this internal analysis, the critical success factors for RINL were identified as raw material security,
timely completion & commissioning of projects, new markets & value added products, leadership at every level
and sustainable development.
This report contains the approved Vision statement for RINL which focusses on harnessing the critical success
factors discussed above and achieving the current expansion plans. RINL also came up with a unique value
system to realize their vision along with its objective.
Based on the internal and external environment study of RINL and its identified strengths, weaknesses,
opportunities and threats, RINL needs to adopt various strategic options under themes like Expansion Strategy,
Technology Strategy, Funding Strategy, Project Management Strategy, Commercial Strategy, Raw Material
Strategy, Logistics & Distribution Strategy, Outsourcing Strategy, Human Resource Management Strategy,
Power Strategy, Water Strategy, Energy Efficiency Strategy and Safety, Health & Environment Strategy. The
various strategic options for RINL categorized under the above themes in the reports are:
        Geographical diversification through Greenfield project
        Inorganic growth through acquisition of existing plants
        Continuous upgradation and innovation in technology
        Fund expansion by taking further loans at competitive rates through enhanced credit worthiness
        Timely completion of projects to avoid time & cost overruns
        Control over up-stream and down-stream supply chain to increase market share of products
        Production of in-demand & short supply products
        Long term contracts/futures for raw materials
        Captive mines in India or acquisition of mines/JVs abroad for raw materials
        Combination of rail and sea routes for transportation of iron ore and pellets
        Use of inland and coastal waterways
        Development of captive jetty at Vizag
        Outsourcing of Non – Core Functions
        Align organizational structure with strategy and expansion plans
        Develop a proactive manpower planning system
        Develop and implement a change management strategy to transform work culture
        Setting right people’s accountability to develop leaders at all levels and enhance organizational
         efficiency
        HR manual for implementation of HR policies & procedures
        Up gradation of employee skills through training
        Sustainable Power, Water, Energy, Safety, Health and Environment strategy


Each strategic option has been further elaborated with context & drivers, associated risks, case studies of
competitors adopting similar strategies, classified under short, medium, long term and finally
recommendations/ action plan to implement these strategies have been provided.

The report has projected profit and loss statement and the balance sheet as well the cash flow statements of
RINL till 2027. They have been provided along with the major financial ratios (profitability ratio, liquidity
ratios, etc.) keeping in mind the expansion plans of RINL and the various strategic options with financial
implication.

The implementation of these strategic options would require RINL to take up various actions with immediate
effect. Such urgent actions, spread across multiple functions like Sourcing & Procurement, Operations,
Marketing & Sales, Finance and Human Resource, have also been discussed along with responsibility and time

2. Introduction
2.1. Background
Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd (RINL), wholly owned company by the Government of India, commenced operations
in 1982 and was granted the Navaratna status in 2010. The company began its operations with a saleable
capacity of 2.6 million tons per annum (MTPA) at Vishakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh.

The company's product range comprises wire rods, rounds, angles, channels, beams, squares, blooms, saleable
billets, pig iron, coal chemicals, granulated slag and other by-products. These products are used by the
construction, infrastructure, railways, power, oil, defense, transport and ship-building sectors. Wire rods are
used in the wire drawing industry.

RINL is currently in a growth phase. Commissioning and stabilization activities of new facilities have already
commenced to expand the current capacity to 6.3 MTPA. Next phase of expansion, for expanding plant capacity
by 1 MTPA through modernization programs, is already on and is likely to be achieved by FY 2016 -17. Further,
the Board approval is awaited for expansion till 12 MTPA which was expected to be achieved by 2019-20 now
revised to FY 2020-21. The ultimate aim of RINL was to achieve 20 MTPA capacity by 2027 which has now
been revised to FY 2033.

In view of the major shifts in external scenario and expansion plans, RINL wants to revisit its Corporate Plan
2020 made in the year 2007 and formulate Vision 2027 - Corporate Plan document. PwC was selected through
a competitive bidding process for developing the “Corporate Plan-Vision 2027” document for RINL.
Subsequently it was decided to rename the document as “Corporate Plan – Vision 2025” document for RINL.

3. External Business Environment- Trends
3.1. Global steel industry scenario
Steel is an important engineering material because of its extensive use in strategic areas such as defense, power,
atomic energy, and in creation of social and economic infrastructure which are essential for a nation’s economic
security. The main features of the global steel industry is as follows
     The global steel industry is cyclic in nature and has seen highs and lows with changing economic scenario.
     Earlier, global steel industry was predominately controlled by today’s developed nations but since late 90’s,
      rapid economic growth in China has shifted the balance. China has emerged as largest steel producing
      country being followed slowly and steadily by India. With China increasing its production and consumption
      of crude steel by 460% and 370% respectively during 2000-2012, steel market has skewed towards Asian
      Economies which at present and in future shall drive the global crude steel demand.
     In the recent past there has been high volatility in the prices of steel and major raw materials like coal and
      iron ore. This has impacted the margins of various steel producers. As a result of this volatility, steels
      makers are now moving to a monthly or quarterly pricing mechanism in place of the earlier annual prices.
     The global steel industry has been facing the problems of accumulation of excess capacity resulting in low
      utilization. As a response to this scenario, in the last two decades, the industry has taken to consolidation
      through mergers or acquisitions with other players.

Despite the increase in global demand for steel and the removal of some older steelmaking capacity in 2012,
steel players have been operating in a challenging environment with rising input costs and persistent lower
capacity utilization. Excess capacity is greater now than it was a year ago due to the continued growth in new
steelmaking facilities particularly in developing economies. Thus, capacity utilization rates have remained
below 80%, and in 2014 excess capacity will remain the most significant issue in the steel sector. Low demand
growth in developed markets, accompanied by a structural shift in the global steel industry to developing
countries like China and India further compounds the challenges for the steel players.
Growth in global steel demand is unlikely to improve significantly in the near future. Overall, the developing
and emerging economies had seen their steel demand growing by 3.0% and 3.7% in 2012 and 2013 respectively,
whereas in the developed world, steel demand was expected to contract by 0.3% in 2012 and then grow by 1.9%
in 2013. Sluggish demand combined with excess steelmaking capacity and ongoing volatility in raw materials

7.2. Technology Strategy
Context and drivers
Steel making process adopted at RINL is through BF-BOF route - the most common steel making process for an
integrated steel plant. RINL had adopted the then state of the art technologies at 3 MTPA stage and green
technologies at every stage of operation has been a major source of competitive advantage to the company in
the area of operational efficiency. The same has now emerged as a driver for profitability for the company in
view of prevailing high cost of raw materials and sluggishness in markets that inhibits passing on the costs to
customers.

Sustaining competitive advantage in the area of operational efficiency is a strategic imperative for RINL, as:

         Cost structure of the company depends critically on it in view of huge disadvantage that the company
          suffers from due to lack of captive sources of major raw materials and

         Parity being gained by competitors who are in the process of infusing new technologies / adopting
          latest technologies as part of their modernization / expansion plans.
Till middle of the decade of 2000’s, technology was seen as one of the major drivers for cost leadership strategy
in Indian steel industry. However post 2007-08, changed trajectory of raw material prices to higher level,
technology as strategic driver for cost leadership in steel industry has lost its significance and raw material costs
has emerged as single biggest driver for cost leadership.

    Focus on project management capabilities – so that the risk of time and cost over-runs is avoided.

fuels. In addition, Academic Institute like IIT, Kharagpur, IIT, Kanpur and others are also engaged in carrying

In order to ensure efficient project delivery so as to commission and stabilize expansion units at the earliest, the
following set of actions may be taken by RINL:

    Exhaustive risk identification at the planning stage: Most companies don’t conduct detailed risk
     assessment at the planning stage. Each project has some specific risks related to the surrounding
     environment, contractors and local stake holders that could impact project completion. Thus, there is need
     to do a very detailed analysis of all possible risks. Further, these risks need to be formally documented and
     monitored at each stage of project execution.

    Develop Integrated Project Delivery Schedule: Most projects are being executed by split package
     modes in which multiple contractors are carrying out different scope. Further, each contractor submitted its
     own schedule which is generally not integrated to make a single project schedule. The monitoring is carried
     out based on individual schedules. In this system if one contractor is delaying, the effect will not be seen on
     activities of other contractors. Thus, to monitor the project with multiple contractors, it is very important
     to have one a single integrated project schedule encompassing the scope of all contractors. Additionally,
     this schedule has to be updated frequently to monitor overall project status.

    Build power partnership with vendors: Delay in getting equipment from suppliers/contractors is
     another reason which impacts the project delivery. Building a long term relationship with vendors could
     help in timely delivery of equipment. Further, joint evaluation of project by project owners and the
     contractors can help in identifying the bottlenecks and taking corrective actions.

     related to a project directly report to the Project Executive Director (ED). For e.g. project department,

     o    Early identification of issues & risk: The PMO regularly and independently tracks the status of
          the projects and identifies bottlenecks and risks that may impact project delivery.

           There is always a risk of default by one contractor that can lead to overall delay in project.
          Project Integration: The project is being executed in split package mode and hence the risk
           of integrating project activities comes on NTPC. Individual contractors will perform their
           piece of work and will be responsible for completing their scope only. Any issues relating to
           coordination between activities of two contractors and ensuring performance of the plant as a
           whole lies with NTPC.

           project to logistics and transport related issues. There is huge vehicular traffic on the roads
           connecting to the plant site due to proximity to NCL mines and other industrial area. Poor
           road connectivity & heavy traffic lead to longer transportation time affecting the work.

          Project Monitoring & Reporting system in place at the project site: The project
           team has a dedicated monitoring and reporting team at site under Head – Planning & Systems
           (P&S), which reports directly in to the Project Planning & Monitoring Group (PPMG) at NTPC
           corporate. Following reports are generated for the purpose of reporting project progress:
           o Daily Progress Report (DPR): The DPR contains package-wise progress as against
               monthly planned quantities. The report was generated by respective package engineers
               and submitted to P&S team, which compiles the report for circulation. The DPR also has
               separate section for work done in critical packages, which is also sent to users via SMS.
           o Weekly Progress Report (WPR): WPR is package-wise report on weekly work done
               as against monthly plan. The report contains detailed information on work completed on
               critical packages.
           o Monthly Progress Report: The monthly progress report contains detailed project
               status report containing information on the project progress, milestones completed and
               target completion for the project. This report is generated by PPMG team in head office.

           positions; by either making payments directly to their sub-contractors or at times giving them
           advance payments. These payments are settled against the contractor bills and are helpful in
           maintain the construction pace, thus avoiding delays.
          Logistic Management: To overcome logistic issues related to road transport, NTPC relied
           on railways to transport its material. Further, to make railway mode economical, NTPC
           consolidated the supplies of different contractors at one place, sufficient for a full load train.

Branding
A brand defines the value of a product to be delivered to the consumer and helps in differentiating this value
from that of other same or similar products in the market. This differentiation helps in creating a distinguished
market identity for the product and getting preference from customers. A strong brand acts as a customer’s tool
for making a good choice in complex, risky or confusing market situations. A strong brand sells itself and helps
to reach to a number of small businesses which may not be economically possible using the direct sales force.
Branding also helps to prevent ad hoc marketing of the same product by different retailers. Ad hoc marketing
creates confusion among customers and may reflect on the company and affect sales. Moreover, retailers do not
have a brand of their own and need a brand to promote themselves. Customers are also comfortable buying
products from retails which represent a strong brand. Branding can also help in building customer
relationships which can help to reduce the impact of competition from low-priced secondary producers to
certain extent. A strong brand also helps in realizing higher margins as the value promised by the brand reduces
the risk of the customer. Branding helps in preventing commoditization of steel products which increase
competition and impacts the margins.
RINL should take up an extensive exercise for branding its products and promotion of branded products.
Almost all steel players in across the globe are giving special focus to branding of their products. RINL should
place its branded products against the branded products of its competitors in order to improve its market share.
The major steps to be taken for this exercise are:

Pre-branding tasks

           determining the broad scope and extent of branding.

      2. Review of products based on the technical specifications, flexibility, customer requirements, quantity
         requirements, etc. It is advisable to go for branding of products where there are similar technical
         specifications, low demand for customization and large quantity requirements of similar products.

Branding tasks

      3. Branding of products selected from the above step. For this RINL shall have to take requisite
         regulatory and legal steps. This should be done with the help of professional external agencies.

      4. Launching of Brand- This needs to be done in a well planned and organized manner so as to gain
         maximum leverage in terms of market presence with relevant customers.

      5.   Promotion of Brand- RINL will be required to form a special team for different brands that shall carry
           out the promotion and marketing of brands at an extensive level. A good promotion will lead to a
           strong and successful brand.

Post-branding tasks

      6. Brand assessment- It is of utmost importance to analyze the performance and strength of the brand
         from time to time in order to evaluate the branding exercise. This shall not only help in determining
         the level of success of the brand but shall also help in developing further action plans to increase the
         strength of the brand. This can be carried out by an external agency which shall evaluate the various
         brands of RINL at a pre defined frequency.

Action V: Increasing exports – Exports to regions like South East Asia, Middle East
and Africa
From 2006-2012 world steel usage grew by 24% and the major contributors to this growth are developing
regions like Asia (49% growth), Middle East (42% growth) and Africa (33% growth). China and India witnessed
a growth 71% of 57% respectively during this period. But, during the same period some of the major developed
regions have witnessed negative growth in terms of steel usage like European Union (25% decline) and NAFTA
(15% decline). Most of the developing economies like Asian markets have shown an increasing trend during the
above period irrespective of the global economic slump in the middle of this period which impacted the global
steel usage.
According to the estimates of World Steel Association and PwC analysis, the global steel consumption is
expected to reach 2168 MT by 2027. The major driver of this rise shall be demand from Asian region with its
share in steel consumption rising from the level of 68% (2011) to around 73% in 2027. Demand from India is
expected to grow by 223% till 2027 at a high CAGR of 7.6%. Steel consumption in Africa is also expected to
grow by 118% by 2027. Countries under ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) and MENA (Middle
East and North Africa) have been largely dependent on imports to meet their steel requirements. Given the
growth in demand and dependence on imports, many players have started opening production facilities in these

7.6. Raw Material Strategy
Presently, raw material cost forms nearly two thirds of the total cost structure of RINL including cost of Iron
Ore, Coking Coal and other raw materials. At the existing capacity of 3.3 MTPA, the combined raw materials
requirement is nearly 10 MTPA. With the expansions planned, the raw material requirement shall be around
20MTPA in the near future and shall go up to nearly 60 MTPA with a capacity of 20 MTPA finished steel.
Steel producers, who own mines or have firm linkages for procuring raw materials, have higher operating
margins as compared to those players who do not own mines due to purchase on market prices and are thus,
subject to market uncertainties with respect to raw materials supply as well as pricing. The volatility in price
and availability of raw materials may also pose a threat to such players in the future.
In recent years, Indian steel industry has grown at a better pace as compared to the developed nations and is
expected to grow at a higher rate in the future. While demand is expected to increase, supply is expected to
increase at higher pace than demand. Thus, increased capacity additions will intensify competition for steel
market as well as procurement of raw material. Given the increasing competition, the profit margins of RINL
may be affected. It is therefore a high priority matter to have a robust and effective strategy to:

     Ensure availability of raw materials at economical prices
     Reduce the percentage of raw material cost in the total cost structure of RINL

Pelletisation plants along with Captive Mines
Indian steel firms predominantly used lump ore over iron ore fines as they had easy access to good quality iron
ore lumps. Iron ore fines cannot be used directly to make hot metal and converted into usable agglomerates like
sinters and pellets. Easy availability of iron ore lumps has resulted in the pellet industry being neglected so far.
As hard ore reserves are depleting day by day, lump generation suitable for blast furnace operation is coming
down resulting in production of large amount of surplus fines. The share of lumps in total iron ore production
declined from 47% in 2006-07 45% in 2010-11 and is expected to further decline to 38% by 2015-16. As fines
shall form considerable part of iron ore produced, value addition to the iron ore fines through various activities
such as beneficiation, pelletisation is the need of the hour.
Pellets are agglomerates of iron ore fines or slimes having high iron content and uniform quality. They are
highly porous and have better reducibility than sinter or iron ore lumps. The heat required for pelletisation is
only two thirds of that required for sintering. Pellets have high strength and can be transported to long
distances. Use of pellets also reduces the coal consumption in blast furnace. The use of pellet in blast furnace in
India is quite less and presently pellets form nearly 10-15% of the iron ore mix. However, since the availability
of lump ore is reducing, a need for charging pellets in place of hard lump has been felt by the industry and some
of the units have already started using more pellets. The share of pellets in average iron ore mix in India is

Use of low grade iron ore
Given that steel plants in India have been using iron ore of Fe content greater than 62%, lower grade resources
were typically less demanded. Further, the threshold grade declared by IBM was at 55% Fe content and thus
miners resorted to selective mining leaving iron ore resources below 58%- 60% in ground to the extent possible
while resources mined as part of mining process are staked at the mine mouth.
As per Justice M B Shah Report on Illegal mining of iron ore and chromite, based on the current rate of
production, the life indices of the high grade lumpy ore (hematite) will be 10 years. If there is further
exploration of iron ore resources, at the most, iron ore reserves would be exhausted within 57 years.
The Indian Bureau of Mines has identified that significant quantities of low-grade iron ore fines are generated
from operating mines which have not been utilized adequately. These are either lying in heaps or are being used
for various non-metallurgical uses such as filling up pits and building roads.
Apart from this, significant quantity of slimes is generated (approximately 20-25% of ROM) during the wet
processing of iron ores. These slimes that are normally dumped in the tailings ponds have led to their
accumulation over the years. NMDC for instance has 20 MT of iron ore in its tailings pond. These are
considered as an environmental hazard as the risk of these slimes causing water pollution in the vicinity areas is
high. The efficient exploitation of these slimes will not only increase the iron ore availability but also solve the
problems of environmental degradation.

Long term contracts/futures to hedge against price volatility

Context and drivers
Presently, RINL procures almost all its raw materials from the market at market prices. RINL procures iron ore
at the market price of NMDC. Coking coal is procured at FOB price from source country which is revised every
quarter or every month in case of certain suppliers. Further, RINL pays the logistics cost (shipping cost) at the
prevailing market price. Given the high volatility in the prices of raw material and ocean freight, RINL can go
for Future Contracts for procurement of commodities and logistics services to hedge the risks of such volatility.
A Futures contract is a standardized contract, traded on a Futures exchange, that commits the holder to buy or
sell a given quantity and quality of an underlying asset or commodity or service on a specified date in the future,
at a price level agreed at the time of the trade. A Futures contract gives the buyer an obligation to buy the
underlying asset should they hold the position past the expiry date of the contract. A seller of a Futures contract
has an obligation to sell the underlying asset should they hold the position past the expiry date of the contract.
Both parties of a Futures contract must fulfill the contract on the settlement date as laid down by the exchange.
At expiry, cash is transferred from the Futures trader who sustained a loss to the one who made a profit. To exit
the commitment prior to the settlement date, the holder of a Futures position will offset their position by taking
an equal but opposite position in the Futures market, with the same delivery date and based on the same asset.
The objective of Futures hedging is to remove the uncertainty of future spot prices by locking in the fixed price
with a Futures contract for a specific time period. The hedger can hold the contract until expiry and make/take
payment against the index value, or exit the Futures position by taking an equal and opposite position. In both
cases the profit/loss offsets the gain/losses incurred when covering the physical requirements in the spot
market.
Various types of contracts available in the market are:
•    Over-the-counter (OTC) contracts - bilateral contracts for two parties come to terms about how a
     specific agreement is to be settled in the future.
•    Index-Linked Forward contracts: A forward contract with price not fixed but linked to an agreed price
     index during period of delivery.
•    Swaps: paper hedging instrument for end-user to secure price that paid to a financial institution and in
     turn get payments on the market price.
•    Spreads: buying or selling the differential between contract prices of two different periods or differential
     between prices of two related products
•    Fixed price forward contract: a standardized contract to sell and buy physical commodity with delivery
     deferred beyond the transaction date.
Futures for iron ore and coal are majorly being offered by CME Group, Singapore Exchange (SGX) and
Intercontinental Exchange (ICE). These futures are based on indexes and are settled financially than with the
raw material. Futures are also available for freight to hedge against fluctuation in freight rates for imported raw
materials. Futures for finishes steel products are also offered by these exchanges. Various iron ore futures are
offered by CME, SGX and ICE. Recently, China has launched iron ore futures for physical delivery on China’s
Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE).

Associated risks
The major risk involved in a Futures Contract is when the market prices of the commodity are lower than the
prices fixed in the Futures Contract. This causes the company to pay more for the same commodity which is
available at a cheaper price in the market. Therefore, a thorough understanding and insight of the market is
required to have a comprehensive forecast of the market based on which a Futures Contract can be entered.

7.7. Logistics & Distribution Strategy
RINL is a coast based plant. Currently, it imports all its coking coal and limestone requirements through the
Gangavaram port due to its close proximity. Iron ore is transported from Bailadila mines of NMDC to Vizag via

RINL has embarked on capacity expansion that will require additional quantity of raw material. The quantity of
coking coal imported is estimated to increase to 15.3 MTPA by 2028-29. Similarly, the import of limestone is
estimated at 2.7 MTPA by 2028-29. Iron ore requirement is also expected to increase significantly. For this, it
has applied for 29 iron ore mining applications in various states. Only one has materialized so far, in Bhilwara,

Use of inland and coastal waterways

India is blessed with 7,551km of coastline and about 14,500km of navigable inland waterways. Yet this sector
has remained neglected despite universal acceptance that transportation through waterways, both coastal and
inland, is fuel efficient, environment friendly and more economical than rail and road. India transports only 7%
of its domestic cargo by coastal shipping while the European Union transports 42%, China 43% and US 15%.
Inland water transport accounts for less than a 1% share of goods transported within India. Of the navigable
inland waterways, 4,503km are national waterways.

Earlier, provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act pertaining to construction, equipment, operation, certification
and safety applicable to vessels plying in international waters were mandatory in all respects to vessels plying
exclusively in the coastal trade. As a result, coastal ships were subject to the same stringent construction and
safety standards as those of ocean-going vessels. These provisions were relaxed in 2011. On 31st July 2013, the
Directorate General of Shipping (DGS) granted further exemptions to Indian ships exclusively carrying cargo on
local routes. This relaxation is now being significantly expanded to cover more ships and opens up
opportunities for utilization of inland and coastal waterways.

                                  Exploiting inland and coastal waterways: NTPC Ltd.
In 2011, NTPC Ltd. awarded a seven-year contract to Jindal ITF Ltd for transporting 3 MTPA of imported
coal from Sandheads (Bay of Bengal) to its thermal power plant located at Farakka through the Haldia-
Farakka waterway. It has floated a second tender for a 10-year contract to haul 3 MTPA of imported coal
through inland waterways to its power project at Barh in Bihar. It is also seeking a similar arrangement to
transport 1.5 MTPA of imported coal to its thermal power station at Bongaigaon in Assam.

RINL can explore this opportunity for transportation of raw materials and steel products within India.

              these grades into levels/bands with no reporting relationships between these bands. This
              would ensure rapid and effective communication flow and quick decision making and hence reducing
              the cycle time for all processes. The decision making can also be supported by group decision
              support system.

  Develop and Implement A Change Management Strategy to

Context and drivers
Transformation of work culture is a critical process to enhance the accountability of all personnel and in turn
enhance organizational effectiveness. The human side of change management includes alignment of the
company’s culture, values, people, and behaviors — to encourage the desired results. Plans themselves do not
capture value; value is realized only through the sustained, collective actions of the employees who are

7.13. Solid Waste Management
Context and drivers

As per the statistics of steel industry an average of about 500 Kg of solid by products is generated in the steel
industry per tonne of crude steel. Major share of this consists of Blast Furnace Slag and basic Oxygen Furnace
Slag. These wastes are an ecological hazard because these degrade the soil quality as well as the water table.
In a steel industry, all the three types of waste materials (gaseous, liquid and solid) are generated. The
generation of gaseous waste material is the highest but the management of solid waste material is the most
talked about issue.
Now out of the solid wastes a few research programmes have been initiated sporadically but still a considerable
percentage is dumped because of unusability. The dumping of solid wastes consumes about 10 hetres of land (1
ha = 2.4 acres) per million ton of waste generation. So it is quite imaginable that high chunk of land would be
wasted if this problem is not addressed seriously. Hence the big volume of land owned by RINL –which is felt
enough for 20 Mnt expansions may be inadequate in future for pilling of large volumes of solid wastes.

7.14. Safety, Health & Environment Strategy
Context and drivers
RINL has been a pioneer in adoption of green/clean technologies like Coke dry quenching, LD gas recovery,
evaporative cooling system & waste heat recovery from furnace, etc. during inception even when the concept of
green manufacturing was at a nascent stage. Though pollution control mechanisms and facilities to recycle
waste energy are generally integrated with plant operations, exclusive departments exist for centralised
monitoring of the same. In the current timeframe, RINL is focused on execution of various zero discharge which
would further lower water intake.
The plant is certified for EMS but opportunity exists in the form of adopting the concepts of Sustainable
Development and spread good practices beyond the company (along the supply chain). Plant has distinguished
itself in adoption of green technologies however more thrust may be required to utilize the potential and more
rigour can be applied for unearthing the opportunities for improvements through intensive energy audits,
energy value streams etc. Plant needs to focus on taking maximum advantage from PAT and CDM. Though
safety checks and audits are in place, the company needs to spread a culture of safe working in the long run.
Environment
Steel industry across the globe, and particularly in the advanced countries have identified climate change as a
major challenge for more than two decades and have been proactive in reducing energy consumption and green
house gas emissions by aggressive R&D and Technology intervention adopting the clean & green and state-of-
art technologies in all areas of production.
Chinese and Indian Steel industry roughly account for about 50% of world steel production and are high in
energy intensity and CO2 emission. Although some steps have been taken to curb the pollution but still it is a
long way to go for achieving desired level.
RINL needs to develop its environmental policy with focus on care for the environment and compliance with
applicable regulations. The following activities are suggested as a part of RINL’s environmental responsibilities:

         Water supply for irrigation to nearby villages
         Undertaking planting of saplings in and around the plant area and development of green-belt within
          the premises
         Noise and energy reduction activities within the plant and at employee residences
         Increasing awareness towards environment protection to the local people
The following technological developments in line with those adopted abroad are suggested to be the long term
objective:

         Coal: minimize coal consumption by adopting oxygen operation in modified BF/ Smelting Reduction
          like Finex or similarly designed furnaces alongwith in-process CO2 capture rather than oxy-fuel
          combustion and pre/post combustion capture of CO2 and further reduction.
         Hydrogen: to be used as Reducing agent in place of Coal/Coke, partly or fully.
         Electron: to be used as reducing agent like Hydrogen.
         Biomass: to be used to generate reducing gas.
         Carbon Capture & Storage (CCS): to find out ways and means to capture CO2 gas and Store it in deep
          saline aquifers, depleted oil or gas fields, in coal mines as geological storage or turned back into
          carbonate etc.

Preferred group: Joint collaborative research programs involving Government, Steel producers, Consultants,
Technology Providers & Equipment Manufacturers, Academic Institutions, Design Organizations and others.

Sustainable Development

ability of the future generations to meet their own needs. Sustainable development involves an enduring and
balanced approach to economic activity, social progress and environmental responsibility.

Enterprises, all Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSE) are requested to implement with immediate effect on
the following;

Threat of substitute products
Aluminum and plastics & composites pose threat to steel in automotive industry. However, at present the high
cost of electricity for extraction and purification of aluminium in India weighs against viable use of aluminium
for the automobile industry. Steel has already been replaced in some large volume applications like large
diameter water pipes (RCC pipes), small diameter pipes (PVC pipes).
The threat of substitute seems low as the demand for steel will mainly be driven by infrastructure and
construction sectors and it is difficult to substitute steel in these sectors. This is further supported by the growth
projections for the steel industry by various agencies. The infrastructure, construction and engineering and
fabrication sectors combined are estimated to result in 100 MT increase in steel consumption by 2027, which is
about 78% of total net increase estimated.
Further, as discussed earlier, per capita steel use in India is 56.9 kgs which is the lowest among the top 10 steel
producers of the world. It is merely one fourth of the global average. The low per capita consumption of steel in
India indicates the significant potential of increasing the steel consumption and the unexploited rural markets
of the Indian economy presents a good scope of increasing the per capita steel use in the country.

Bargaining power of customers
Presently, RINL produces only longs products although it has plans to enter into flat products in future.
Currently, the producers of long products in India apart from RINL are SAIL, JSWL, JSPL and others (mostly
secondary producers). The share of RINL in production of long products is about 8% and secondary producers
dominate the market.
RINL has three types of customers:

   Industrial sales: These customers are those who take RINL steel for further processing into specific
    products. This accounts for nearly 25% of the total sales. The major products consumed are wire rods,
    squares and rounds. These customers are consistent customers but their demand shall be guided by the
    demand of their end products.

   Project sales: These customers are those who take RINL steel for some major infrastructure projects in
    various sectors of the economy. This accounts for nearly 25% of the total sales. The major products
    consumed are TMT, RE bars, structurals. These customers are one time customers but their demand is
    generally large and therefore they do not go via retailers to increase their bargaining power. Since they will
    be the end users, they will not add any margins as compared to industrial and retail customers.

   Retail sales: These customers are those who take RINL steel for selling in the retail market. Retail sales
    accounts for nearly 50% of the total sales. The major products consumed are TMT, RE bars, structurals.
    Generally, these are consistent customers but their demand is entirely dependent on/vulnerable to the
    market situation.
The share of RINL in the Indian market has seen a continuous decline in the last 5-6 years. Two major factors
that contributed to this decline are JSW and other producers. During the last 5-6 years, JSW has almost
doubled its production. Being located in the Southern region, JSW has increased the alternatives for customers
in Southern region. This is evident from the decrease in RINL’s Southern market share and profits. The
production by other players which mainly comprise of small to medium scale, low technology driven units
(mainly producing long products), has grown by 50% in the last 5-6 years. This increase in availability of low
cost long products has increased the bargaining power of customers by providing them cheap alternatives.

Bargaining power of suppliers
Iron ore: The large resource base of iron ore in the country indicates that presently, India is self sufficient in
meeting the demand of iron ore. Although, in last 1-2 years, the iron ore production in country has reduced
significantly but it was more on the account of ban imposed by courts rather than any operational issues. There
are more than 30 companies in iron ore mining of which NMDC is the largest producer (30 MT). Presently,
RINL meets its complete requirement of iron ore from NMDC. Other customers of NMDC include KIOCL, Essar
Steel, JSW Ispat, Visvesarya Iron and Steel Limited, Southern Iron and Steel Company Limited etc. The
capacity expansion plans of NMDC to increase its mining capacity from 30 MT to 50 MT by 2016 may reduce
uncertainties of supply of iron ore to RINL in medium term but in longer term it may need to look at other
captive sources/strategic tie-ups, considering the projections of significant increase in iron ore demand in
future (392 MT by 2025-26 as per draft NSP 2012).
Further, the major concern for the steel manufacturers is to have captive sources. The raw material security
conferred by captive mines offers availability and lower input costs with the potential price escalation and
market volatility taken out of the equation. The analysis of cost structure of key domestic steel producers shows
that the share of raw material cost in total operating expenses is more than 2/3rd in case of companies with non-
captive sources and less than 40% in case of companies with captive sources. Currently, the iron ore prices are
determined by NMDC and RINL does not have much power to negotiate it.
Thus, currently the suppliers have large bargaining power and it is in the best interest of steel producers to
develop their own iron ore assets.
Coking coal: For coking coal, there is scarcity of domestic sources and Indian steel companies significantly
depend on imports, largely from Australia (more than 75%) followed by USA, South Africa, Mozambique, New
Zealand, Canada etc. As per the AME reports, the metallurgical coal demand (imports) is led by China (25% of
global metallurgical import demand) followed by Japan (24%) and India (11%). If we look at the supply side,
Australia is the largest exporter (56% of total world exports) of metallurgical coal followed by USA (19%) and
Canada (10%).
Thus, it may be concluded that the global demand-supply and prices of coking coal are mainly driven by
Australia, China and Japan. Since, India does not have very significant share in global coking coal and is largely
dependent on Australia for imports; it may be assumed that Indian consumers have to be price takers rather
than price makers.
Further, the large dependence on imports exposes the Indian producers to the risks related to the changing
regulatory scenario in other countries. For example, in Indonesia, on one hand, Domestic Market Obligations
impose the limit on coal to be traded internationally while on the other hand, price benchmarking is expected to
increase the price of coal. Similarly, in Australia provisions for MRRT and Carbon Tax increase the price of coal
to consumers.
This necessitates the requirement of intensive efforts in increasing supplies from other avenues, like
Mozambique, Columbia. But, there are numerous challenges in these countries ranging from lack of
infrastructure to export coal out of country, concerns over stability of political and fiscal regime, unavailability
of skilled manpower, etc. Thus, beyond acquiring mineral assets, huge investment in developing surrounding
infrastructure and government support to secure stable fiscal regime would be necessary to ensure long term
sustainable coal imports from these countries.

The availability or lack of captive raw material sources creates very particular risks and challenges for steel

most of the magnetite resources are in environmentally sensitive Western Ghats and adjoining areas and
exploitation of these will be difficult with the declaration of the Western Ghats as World Heritage Site.
Currently, several companies are planning for new capacity addition in India and many of the projects are
expected to be green-field projects. These faces direct risk of delays on account of difficult R&R issues and
political actions. At the state level, there is lack of a clear R&R policy and investors are left to work the system

In addition to above factors, recently approved Land Acquisition Act, is expected to increase cost of land
acquisition resulting in higher project cost impacting project viability. The new Act requires consent of atleast
70% and 80 % of the potential land losers in case of public-private partnership (PPP) projects and private
projects respectively. Further, it requires 40 % profit sharing with the original owner in case land is sold to a
third party for a price higher than the compensation paid.
The corporate sector also needs to put more focus on its corporate social responsibility strategy. This may
involve defining first a business case for sustainability, assessing its sustainability management practices and
identifying gaps in practice vis-à-vis the best practices.
The above mentioned factors have impacted the investor confidence and companies are trying to find new
locations for their projects e.g. POSCO has now decided to invest in Brazil and Indonesia.
There is a need for a clear statement of intent by Governments, supported by broader political consensus, on
how they will support sector development, in the interest of the nation. The National Steel Policy 2012 (Draft)
provides direction to remove bottlenecks with measures proposed for increasing transparency, raw materials
security, improving infrastructure etc. but considering the ground realities, implementing this directional plan
is a big challenge.

Economic Factors
As with rest of the world economy, India experienced low growth due to the global financial crisis in 2008-09.
Due to the strong fundamentals, Indian economy was able to achieve a high growth rate of 8.6 per cent and 9.3
per cent respectively in 2009-10 and 2010-11, post crisis. However, over the past two years the growth rates
have been on decline with the raise in policy rates by Reserve Bank of India (RBI) impacting investments. The
growth rate has halved in just three years and RBI as expects GDP to growth at 4.8% in 2013-14.
As per the Economic Survey 2012, the decline in growth rate is primarily attributable to weakness in industry
(comprising the mining and quarrying, manufacturing, electricity, gas and water supply, and construction
sectors) which registered a growth rate of only 3.5 per cent and 3.1 per cent in 2011-12 and 2012-13 respectively.

Technological Factors
Long products
The continuous casting or strand casting operation produces billets, blooms blanks, and near-net shape
profiles. These semi-finished products are utilized in the rolling mills to produce structural shapes like rods and
bars, wire rods and other structural products like angle beam or channels.
Flat Products
Flat product rolling mills can be broadly categorized into two groups, i.e., hot rolling mills and cold rolling
mills. Plate mills and strip mills fall in the category of hot rolling mills whereas cold reduction mills and skin
pass or temper mills constitute the cold rolling mills. The rolling mills are also categorized in various other
ways, e.g., continuous, semi continuous, tandem or reversing/non-reversing mills depending on equipment
arrangement and 2-hi, 3-hi, 6-hi, 20-hi etc., depending on configuration of rolls in the mills housing.
The technological requirement in case of long products is less as compared to flat products. The status of
technology in India in the flat products rolling mill industry is a unique blend of old and new technologies. Up-
gradation/modernization of the plants is gradually taking place with a view to increase mill productivity,
improvement in yield and product quality, production of diverse range of value-added products and
conservation of depleting energy resources. Regarding technology absorption in the operating plants, it can be
said that by and large the technologies have been successfully absorbed and adapted to Indian working
conditions.

Overview
POSCO is the largest fully integrated steel producer in Korea, and one of the largest steel producers in the world

producers in the world and strive to rank among the top three global steel companies in technology leadership,
operational excellence and production capacity.
Apart from steel making, the company has diversified interests in energy, construction and materials sectors.

Operations
POSCO has been carefully seeking out promising investment opportunities abroad, primarily in China, India,
Southeast Asia and Mexico which are expected to offer substantial growth. Besides these, it is also building
upstream facilities in Indonesia and Brazil, as well as downstream facilities that are tailored to the local
demands.
POSCO’s strategy in operations has been to enhance efficiency of operations and decrease costs through
company-wide process innovation. Since 2001, it has implemented several process innovation initiatives such
as POSPIA, Six Sigma standard master plan and Quick Six Sigma standard master plan which helped to
reorient its business transaction processes including purchase of raw materials and sale of goods to focus on its
customers and established a computerized resource management system. These initiatives along with company-
wide inventory management system substantially cut operational inefficiencies. Production scheduling lead
time fell from 60 days to 15 days, allowing it to shorten the delivery time for hot rolled steel from 30 days to 14
days.

POSCO sales strategy has been to devote its production primarily to satisfy domestic demand, while seeking
export sales to utilize capacity to the fullest extent and to expand its international market presence. Although
supplying the Korean domestic market is its top priority, it intends to continue to supply a significant amount of
its products to customers in overseas markets. This is because:

Annexure 6: Case Study – Tata Steel
Overview
Tata Steel was founded as Tata Iron and Steel Company by Dorabji Tata in 1907 as part of his father Jamsetji ’s
Tata Group. The pig iron production in India began in December 1908 by the TISCO plant in Jamshedpur. The
first ingot of steel was made in 1912 and by 1939 TISCO operated the largest steel plant in the British Empire.
Tata Steel has the credential of developing first integrated steel plant in Asia.
The acquisition of NatSteel in 2004 was Tata Steel’s first overseas acquisition which was followed by a series of
joint ventures and mergers. In April 2007, Tata Steel acquired Corus that created one of the world’s largest
steelmakers, with a major presence in Europe as well as Asia. Presently, Tata Steel Group is among the top-ten
global steel companies with an annual crude steel capacity of over 29 million tonnes per annum. The group has
presence in over 50 developed European and fast growing Asian countries, with manufacturing operations in 26
countries. The group’s has large production facilities in India, the UK, the Netherlands, Thailand, Singapore,
China and Australia. The operating companies within the Group include Tata Steel Limited (India), Tata Steel
Europe Limited (formerly Corus), Tata Steel Singapore and Tata Steel Thailand.
The product portfolio of the company includes flats, longs, tubes, wires and agrico. The company caters to
automotive, appliance, engineering, construction and machinery industries.

Indian operations
In 1907, Tata Steel established India’s first integrated steel plant at Jamshedupr. The Jamshedpur Works
currently has a capacity to produce 9.7 MTPA crude steel production facility and a variety of finishing mills.
Presently, Tata Steel is third largest producer of steel in the country and has the distinction of being the largest
supplier of steel to Indian automotive industry. Tata Steel has a 50:50 joint venture with Bluescope Steel
Australia, namely Tata Bluescope Steel Ltd. (TBSL). TBSL’s coated steel division has a new manufacturing
facility at Bara, Jamshedpur with a capacity to produce 250,000 tonnes per annum in Zinc-Aluminium (Zn-Al)
coated coils. In last financial year, the group generated maximum revenue from India (29%). Tata Steel had
total sales volumes of 7.48 million tonnes in India of which 2.98 million tonnes were long products.

For the Indian operations, about 60% of coking coal requirements and 100% of iron ore requirements are met
from captive sources. The company has following raw material sources:

      Captive iron ore mines located in Noamundi, Joda and Katamati in the states of Jharkhand and Orissa.

      Captive coal mines at Jharia (coking coal) and West Bokaro(semi-coking coal).

      Manganese mines and dolomite quarries in Orissa.

        JV between Tata Steel & Nippon Steel Corporation for implementation of the 0.6 MTPA Continuous

Cost reduction and performance improvement
In addition to organic growth the company is putting efforts to increase efficiency of processes. With an aim to
strengthen its profitability, the company plans cost reduction across all business and operations verticals.
Tata Steel (India) has been able to make significant savings due to the improvement initiatives over the past few
years. In FY 13, the company made savings of Rs 1560 crore, most of which is attributable to Kar Vijay Har
Shikhar (KVHS) initiative.

Kar Vijay Har Shikhar (KVHS) – continuous improvement programme: KVHS is a well-defined six step
process involving TQM and statistical tools. Some of the key themes through which improvements are taken up
are – Throughput, Value-in-use, Energy Efficiency, Opportunistic Plays, Logistics & Supply Chain. In FY 12,
Tata Steel launched KVHS in marketing and sales for the Indian operations while in FY 13, the primary focus
was on mines and production processes in India. Tata Steel has been able to launch several projects like - Load
Haul Dumpers at Jharia Mines, Synthetic Collector for improving Clean Coal yield, Excavator Hanger at West
Bokaro, Desiliconisation trials at Blast Furnaces, TBD Resleeving Machine at LD#1(first time in Asia), Quick
Tap Drop System at LD#1, Seven Roll Feeder installation at SP#3, Micropelletisation Super Fines for use in
Sinter Making, Paving Bricks from LD Slag. Some of these have been implemented while others are in trial
phase. Tata Steel has also added sustainability activities like mine life, solid waste utilization and energy
efficiency to the portfolio of initiatives under KVHS.

Markets
The company is emphasizing towards shift to an enhanced product mix. It has been putting efforts to penetrate
in new market segments like small and medium enterprises. Tata Steel carried out a pan India market mapping
to understand the consumption pockets, patterns and needs of the customers for HR Steel. Tata Steel has
identified this segment as an Emerging Corporate Account (ECA) with a requirement for small tonnages. In
order to better understand the needs of the segment, a structured pilot programme called Emerging Corporate
Value Management (ECVM) was launched. As an outcome of this, Tata Steel mapped 4,500 customers falling
into 37 application based segments and appointed 47 distributors to serve them.
Tata Steel has also continuously worked towards de-commoditising and branding steel. Tata Steel’s brands are
spread across sectors like construction (Tata Tiscon and Tata Structura), roofing (Tata Shaktee), panels &
furniture (Tata Steelium and Galvano) and agricultural implements (Tata Agrico). These brands, put together,
contribute ~30% to the top line of Tata Steel. Tata Steel has recently launched a new brand “Tata Astrum” for
Hot Rolled (HR) Sheets and Coils, to penetrate the SME market.

Raw material security
In order to ensure raw material security, Tata Steel has made investments (through its subsidiaries) in several
countries such as:

In India, the company has plans to set up 6 MTPA pellet plant which will enable the company to use extra-fine
iron ore as the feed instead of scarce lumps, resulting in improved productivity of Blast Furnace. Further, the
company is also working to increase the life of its existing mines by improving productivity and enhancing its
capabilities to mine and process inferior ores.

European Operations
Tata Steel Europe (erstwhile Corus) has a crude steel production capacity of 18 MTPA with manufacturing
operations in Western Europe, plants in UK, Netherlands, Germany, France and Belgium. In UK, the
manufacturing facilities at Tata Steel Europe comprise manufacturing hubs (Strip Products Mainland Europe,
Strip Products UK, Long Products Europe and Downstream Operations) and Integrated Businesses (Plating,
Cogent Power, Speciality and Bar).

The IJmuiden Steel Works in Netherlands is Tata Steel's largest and most cost-efficient steel making facility in
Europe. Presently it has a production capacity of 7.2 MTPA.

Strategies
For the European operations, Tata Steel is focusing on rationalisation of cost base and product differentiation.
It is working towards improving the supply chain capability, IT systems and the product range. The single pan-
European supply chain allocates demand across the manufacturing facilities and distribution channels to
maximise operational efficiencies and minimise costs.

Raw material security

Tata Steel Minerals Canada Limited (TSMC), a joint venture established in October 2010 by Tata Steel Ltd.
(80% stake) and New Millennium Iron Corp (20% stake), is developing the Direct Shipping Ore (DSO) project
involving mining, processing and supplying the sinter fines and pellet fines to Tata Steel's European steel
making facilities. 1 MT production is being targeted this fiscal year and ramp up upto 6 MTPA is planned.

TSMC is also involved with New Millennium Iron Corp. in undertaking a Feasibility Study of the LabMag and
KeMag iron ore deposits.

Markets

During FY 13, Tata Steel in Europe invested in projects to improve product mix and launched 14 new products
with majority in automotive sector. Tata Steel has organised its European business into strategic market sectors
wherein the sector teams develop the commercial plan of the business taking into account its differentiated
product strategy to secure long-term relationships with its customers.

1. Introduction   1


1. INTRODUCTION

Sustainability Plan 2015-16 comprises of Annual Business Plan (ABP) for 2015-16 and medium term roll-on plan
covering the period up to 2019-20 where broad action plans and initiatives beyond the annual timeframe
addressing various aspects related to capacity enhancement, productivity improvement, market development and
initiatives related to HR, CSR, Energy, Environment etc. are addressed. The scope thus extends beyond the
factors contributing to profitability and includes aspects that are important for long term sustainability of the
company.



A PPROACH FOR SUSTAINABILITY PLAN 2015-16:
The process of development of Sustainability Plan 2015-16 was steered by the Apex Committee comprising of all
functional Directors. Apex Committee guided in formulation of MoU targets for 2015-16. Upon finalization of the
same, further guidance was obtained from CMD for setting stretch targets as part of Annual Business Plan.
Accordingly, CMD and Directors reviewed the plan and potential presented by the major departments for finalizing
the Sustainability Plan targets.




R EVIEW M ECHANISM :
      Monthly review by CMD & Directors to be against MoU Plan and Sustainability Plan as well.
      Monthly review by HoDs for exception reporting to CSM.
      Quarterly review of assumptions pertaining to external environment for bringing realistic revision in the
       target/action plans.




                                                          Sustainability Plan 2015-16 & Roll-on Plan till 2019-20   |

2    2. Company Performance in 2014-15


    2. COMPANY PERFORMANCE IN 2014-15

    Expansion to 6.3 Mtpa of liquid steel - all major units of Stage-1 have been commissioned and are under regular
    operation. Special Bar Mill and Structural Mill are commissioned on 3rd Apr’15 and 30th Apr’15 respectively and are
    being fine-tuned for rolling different sizes.
                                              Fig. 2.0: Expansion Units 2014-15
                                            Facility                                   Status

                 Top Recovery Turbine of BF-3 for 14 MW power             Commissioned on 9th Jun’14
                 generation from waste pressure of BF Gas

                 By- product Plant in COB-4                               Commissioned on 13th Dec’14
                 Power Plant-II Boiler-1                                  Lighted up
                 4th Caster, revamp of Sinter Plant, Turbo Blower-5       Orders placed
                 and CDCP for Coke oven Battery-5


    Major highlights for the year 2014-15 include the following:
        Production of 3.3 Mt of Crude Steel achieved - a growth of 3% over CPLY, in spite of production loss on
            account of cyclone. The growth would be about 10% after adjustment for the impact.
        Production of 21.94 lakh tonnes of value added steel - about 73 % of saleable steel.
        Sales Turnover of about ` 11,674 Crs.
        Record Export Sales of ` 865 Crs. (highest since inception) - a growth of 16% over CPLY.
        An International Marketing Office in Sri Lanka was registered.
        Draft Mining Plan submitted to IBM for Banera Iron Ore block allotted by Govt. of Rajasthan Phase-1
        Stabilisation of ERP system introduced in May’14
        Long Term Agreement for 15 years signed with Gangavaram Port Ltd. on 04/08/2014 for handling of Cargo
            and transfer through conveyors.
        Launching of e-learning portal “Gyan Era” for improved learning
        Introduction of new scheme (ASPIRE) to encourage innovative ideas resulting in “breakthrough”
            improvement
        Launching of “Manasulo Mata” - an interactive communication exercise aimed to provide an opportunity
            for a cross section of employees to interact with top management

    Corporate Social Responsibility:
        ` 15.53 Cr has been spent against allocated amount of ` 14.23 Cr.
        Contribution of ` 5Cr to Chief Ministers Relief Fund of Andhra Pradesh in connection to Hudhud

    Swachh Bharat Programme:
        In addition to the planned activities under Corporate Social Responsibility, RINL has taken action for
           construction of 86 toilets in Govt. schools under “SwachhVidyalaya”

4    3. Steel Scenario & Outlook for 2015-16


    3. Steel Scenario & Outlook for 2015-16

    World Steel

    India retained its position as 4th largest producer of steel with a growth rate of 2.3%, which is third highest among
    the top ten producing countries after South Korea (7.5%) and Russia (2.6%). Overall, world steel registered a
    growth of 1.2%.
                                          Fig: 3.0: World crude steel production, Mt
                                   Rank         Country           2013         2014     Growth %
                                      1     China                      815.4    822.7         0.9
                                      2     Japan                      110.6    110.7         0.1
                                      3     USA                         86.9     88.3         1.7
                                     4      India                      81.3      83.2        2.3
                                      5     South Korea                 66.1     71.0         7.5
                                      6     Russia                      68.9     70.7         2.6
                                      7     Germany                     42.6     42.9         0.7
                                      8     Turkey                      34.7     34.0        -1.8
                                      9     Brazil                      34.2     33.9        -0.7
                                     10     Ukraine                     32.8     27.2       -17.1
                                            World                 1642.0       1661.5        1.2



    Indian Steel

           Declining Trend in the share of Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) from 34% in 2011-12 to likely 30%
            in 2014-15 has impacted growth in consumption of steel in the country.
           Growth in apparent consumption in steel has fallen from 10.1% in 2012-13 to 1.4% in 2014-15(Apr-Dec)
           From 2010-11 to 2013-14 , CAGR of capacity addition is 7% and that of real consumption is 4% - capacity
            utilization has declined from 88% in 2010-11 to 82% in 2013-14.
           Surge in imports from Russia, Korea and China (imports of long products increased by 168% in 2014-15)
           Steel prices have crashed since Jun’14 (22% fall in NSR for RINL)


    Outlook for 2015-16
           Apparent steel use expected to grow by 6% in 2015 as a result of recent policy initiatives by GoI
           However, steel capacities likely to lead the growth with 8 to 10 Mt of new capacities in pipeline during the
            year
           Risk of higher imports looms large as India and SE Asia emerge as major export targets, in view of:
                o Distress export by Chinese producers as they grapple with 200Mt of over capacity
                o Strict anti-dumping policies by USA and slower than expected recovery in Euro zone
                o Dampening demand in Middle-East due to softening of crude prices
                o Depreciated Rouble makes Russian imports cheaper
           Profitability will continue to be under pressure with higher debt servicing and working capital cost due to
            expansion /modernization plans

Initiatives for the Year 2015-16:

    1) New sources/ Suppliers of major raw materials:
        To explore the new sources for the supply of Coking Coals, the following initiatives are planned:

             Procurement of industrial trial shipment of 75,000 MT +/- 5% of ‘Tuhup’ Hard Coking Coal from M/s Noble

             An application for additional long term coal linkage of 4.8 lakh tonne per annum due to proposed diversion of BF
             Gas from Power Plant-1 to Power Plant-2 is being submitted.
             Offers received against EOI from other firms are under technical scrutiny.
        b) Global Tender for procurement of Coking Coal
             New global tender for approx.. 5% of Annual requirement Coking Coal for the year 2015-16 has been issued.

             Industrial Trial Shipment of the following Brands are being considered through EJC for the year 2015-16
               ‘North Goonyella’ Coal, Australian Origin from M/s Peabody
               ‘Alpine Coal’, New Zealand Origin from M/s Solid Energy

               ‘Teck Eagle’ Coking Coal, Canada Origin from M/s Lotus Resources (authorized by M/s Teck Coal)

1. Introduction   1



1. INTRODUCTION

Sustainability Plan comprising of various aspects such as capacity enhancement, productivity improvement,
market development and initiatives related to HR, CSR, Energy, Environment etc. with focus on
comprehensive Annual Business Plan (ABP) is prepared every year in the company. The medium term plans
as part of the Sustainability plan document covers broad action plans and initiatives beyond the annual
timeframe, by dovetailing long term goals as milestones spread over next five years in the form of 5 Year
Roll-On Plan. The scope also extends beyond the factors contributing to profitability and includes aspects
that are important from “Sustainability” point of view as well.

    Outlook for 2014-15
    As per India Rating & Research, Jan‟14 report, outlook for domestic steel industry for the year 2014-15 has
    be summarised on following lines:
        Modest improvement in demand expected on the back of modest recovery in economy due to
         infrastructure push by GoI. GDP growth is projected at 5.6% (4.9% in FY 14) and Industrial growth is
         estimated at 4.1% (1.7% in FY 14).
        Limited upside in prices seen as around 13-15 Mt of capacity addition is expected in 2014-15 in
         already prevailing situation of over capacity.
        Globally iron ore prices are set to moderate further as wave of new capacities are slated to hit the
         market. However domestic prices may not follow the trend as demand supply dynamics are very
         different.
        Coking coal prices are expected to be around $160/t as per Metal Expert forecast and Rupee
         depreciation may adversely affect the profitability of steel industry.


    Thrust Areas for Sustainability Plan 2014-15
        Ramp up of production from expansion stream and maximize asset utilization, so as to achieve
         production rates of 6Mt for hot metal, 5.2 Mt for liquid steel and 4.8 Mt for saleable steel in the last
         quarter of the year.
        Develop capability to produce high end value added steel from SMS-2 for improved profitability and
         make in-roads into niche markets.
        Realise full potential of improvement in TE parameters in BF-3 and BF-1 (post CR), which would
         result in substantial and sustainable cost reduction in the company.
        Timely execution of projects for completion of various modernization and expansion projects.
        Strengthen the culture of continuous improvement in the plant that would unlock the latent
         potential for process improvements and cost reduction.
